‼ **AND THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT CARRIED THE BAD INFERENCE SPREAD IT.** I had written the over-claim into
the failure message itself (*"steps_delta … proves the lookup ran"*), so every future reader would
have inherited it. Fixed to state what the counter measures and what it cannot distinguish — the
THIRD over-claiming diagnostic corrected today.


## 2026-09-04 — I PRICED A GRIND AGAINST A FUNCTION THAT COULD NOT DELIVER IT, AND THE ESTIMATE WAS THE ONLY THING I CHECKED

**Symptom.** §Ch23's training leg estimated 438,498 frames / ~306 wild battles to take three battlers
to L47. The run spent its budget and produced **8 battles**: Wailmer 40→41, Mightyena 44→45, Swellow
**+0**. `train_team` returned normally each time, so the leg believed the grind had *finished* and
raised only at its final readiness check.

**Root cause — a position/identity bug inside SHARED code, not in my leg.**
`early_game.py:2021` computes `need` from `party[i]` **by index**. `:2034` then calls
`_rotate_lead_safely(target_slot)`, which drives the party menu's SWITCH option
(`higher_level_actions.py:500`) — a **SWAP**, not a move-to-front. On the next iteration `party[i]`
holds the **old lead** (Sceptile L51 ≥ target), so `need` is empty and the `while True` breaks after
a single spin-batch. ⇒ `train_team(slots={i})` with `i != 0` trains once and reports success.

**The fix that worked, and why it is small.** The bug cannot bite when the mon is *already* slot 0,
because then `target_slot == 0` and no swap happens. So §Ch23 rotates the mon to the lead itself and
hands `train_team` only the case it gets right (`slots={0}`). **A/B on the same fixture:** before,
Wailmer stalled at L41; after, **Wailord reached L47**. Filed as KI-84; deliberately NOT fixed inside
`train_team`, which is also the gym-prep path and would move every gym's levels at once.

**What I actually did wrong.** I had *already written down* the rule this breaks — SESSION DISCIPLINE
#3, *"Assert IDENTITY, never position or count"* — and I applied it scrupulously to MY code: the leg
re-resolves every mon by PID immediately before each call, precisely because rotation invalidates
indices. ‼ **Then I passed those indices into a function I never checked for the same defect.** I
audited my side of the boundary and assumed the other side obeyed a rule I was actively obeying.

**And the estimate hid it.** 438,498 frames was a real number computed from real EXP yields, and it
was *never wrong* — it priced the work correctly and said nothing about whether the executor would do
it. I treated "the plan is affordable" as "the plan will run". ⛔ **A COST MODEL IS NOT A LIVENESS
CHECK.** The guard I built to prevent a runaway grind (KI-28's 19.9M frames) is blind by construction
to the opposite failure: a grind that stops far too early and calls itself done.

**Prevention rules (two, both narrow enough to fire).**
1. ⛔ **WHEN YOU PASS A SLOT INDEX ACROSS A FUNCTION BOUNDARY, THE CALLEE OWNS IT TOO.** Re-resolving
   by identity on your own side proves nothing if the callee re-reads that index after mutating the
   collection. Read the callee's loop before trusting it, or pass the case it cannot get wrong.
2. ⛔ **EVERY LONG-RUNNING CALL NEEDS AN ACHIEVEMENT ASSERT, NOT JUST A BUDGET.** "It returned"
   is not "it worked". §Ch23 now re-reads the mon by PID after each `train_team` and raises if the
   level did not move — the check that would have caught this in one battle instead of 900k frames.


## 2026-09-04 — `gh api | base64 -d` SILENTLY CORRUPTS BINARY DECOMP FILES ON WINDOWS (two agents, independently)

**Symptom.** Two separate research agents fetching pokeemerald layout binaries with
`gh api repos/pret/pokeemerald/contents/<path> --jq .content | base64 -d` received **larger files
than the originals and no error at all**: `VictoryRoad_B1F/map.bin` 2852 bytes decoded to 3942,
`VictoryRoad_1F/map.bin` 4140 decoded to 5756. Both analysed garbage before noticing.

**Root cause.** The pipeline round-trips the decoded bytes through a UTF-16→UTF-8 conversion on
Windows. Any byte that is not valid UTF-8 is re-encoded rather than passed through. Text files
survive; **binaries do not**, and nothing raises.

**The fix that worked.** Fetch binaries from `raw.githubusercontent.com` (e.g. via Python
`urllib`/`requests`), and **verify `len(data) == width * height * 2` against the dimensions in
`data/layouts/layouts.json`** before trusting a single byte. That length check is what caught it
both times — one agent only noticed because the GitHub API's own `size` field disagreed with what it
had received.

**Why this is worth an entry rather than a shrug.** A corrupt layout does not look corrupt. It
decodes into plausible metatile ids, plausible collision bits and plausible elevations, and a
reachability solver run over it returns confident, specific, **wrong** coordinates — which is exactly
the shape this project keeps paying for. One of the two agents also had to correct its own elevation
model mid-run (it propagated with `me or e`, silently swallowing elevation-0 transition tiles and
cutting reachability from 301 tiles to 106), so a decode bug and a model bug can compound invisibly.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **NEVER PIPE BINARY THROUGH `gh api ... | base64 -d` ON WINDOWS. Fetch
binaries from `raw.githubusercontent.com`, and assert the decoded length against an independently
known size before parsing.** A binary read that cannot state its expected length is not a read.


## 2026-09-04 — SIX OF SEVEN §Ch23 FAULT ARMS WERE DEAD FROM CREATION, AND EVERY DOC CALLED THEM PROOF

**Symptom.** A Wally re-test drive died on `BotModeError: Ch23: unknown fault arm 'NOLEAD5'. Known
arms: ['NOHEAL']`. The raise was correct and had been added hours earlier; what it exposed was that
**`NOPIN`, `BADSTEP`, `NOLEAD`, `NOCLIMB`, `NOHEAL4` and `NOLEAD5` had never been registered.**

**Root cause.** `_fault(arm)` builds its env name with an f-string:
`os.environ.get(f"POKEBOT_CH23_FAULT_{arm}")`. An unregistered or mistyped arm therefore reads a
variable nobody sets and returns `False` **forever** — silently, with no error, on every call. Legs
2–5 each shipped a fault hook that **could not fire**, while `29-DISABLED-FEATURES-REGISTRY.md` and
the leg docstrings described those arms as the things that prove the legs' guards work.

⛔ **A FAULT HOOK THAT CANNOT FIRE IS WORSE THAN NO FAULT HOOK: it reads as tested while testing
nothing.** This is the identical shape as `POKEBOT_CH21PROBE_FAULT`'s entry — a probe assertion that
passed because it *could not fail* — recurring in a new place, which is exactly what these entries
exist to stop.

**Why prose did not catch it, and a runtime raise nearly didn't either.** The arms were *documented*
and the call sites were *correct*; the only missing thing was a mapping nobody could see was absent,
because absence produced silence rather than an error. ‼ And the runtime validation that finally
caught it **only fires if someone happens to DRIVE that leg** — it survived until a real Wally run,
and would have survived longer if that run had not been attempted today.

**The fix.** All seven arms registered in `FAULT_ARMS` as arm → full env-name **literal** (the
literal spelling also being what makes `lint_docs` R6 able to see them at all), `_fault` raises on an
unknown arm, and every arm got a registry row. **Then the lesson was made enforceable:**
`tools/story-dev/probe_ch23_fault_arms.py` (gate **#34** in `run_gates.py`) checks statically that every
`_fault(...)` call site is registered, every registered arm is really called, and every arm's env
name is canonical and documented. It walks the **AST**, not a regex, so `_fault("X")` written inside
a comment or docstring correctly does **not** count as a call site — a gate with false positives
teaches the reader to bypass it. Fault-tested three ways (`unregistered` / `orphan` / `noregistry`),
each driving it RED with exit 1; clean exits 0. ‼ Its own first clean run went RED on the
documentation check, and that was a **true** finding: six arms had no registry row.

**Prevention rules.**
1. ⛔ **NEVER BUILD A FLAG NAME BY STRING INTERPOLATION WITHOUT A CLOSED REGISTRY OF THE PARTS.** If
   the parts are computed, an invalid part must RAISE, never return the "off" value — because the
   "off" value is indistinguishable from a correct answer.
2. ⛔ **A SWITCH THAT IS ONLY VALIDATED AT RUNTIME IS VALIDATED ONLY ON THE PATHS SOMEONE RUNS.**
   Anything enumerable — arms, registry rows, call sites — gets a static gate, because the whole
   point of a fault arm is that it is *not* exercised by ordinary runs.
3. ⛔ **WHEN YOU ADD A GUARD AND IT FIRES IMMEDIATELY, THAT IS THE GUARD WORKING — READ WHAT IT
   FOUND BEFORE WEAKENING IT.** The first instinct on seeing a new raise break a drive is to relax
   the new code; here the new code was right and six latent defects were real.


## 2026-09-04 — I INSERTED A GATE MID-LIST, DIRECTLY BENEATH THE TWO WARNINGS THAT FORBID IT

**Symptom.** Adding `probe_ch23_fault_arms.py` to `run_gates.py`, I anchored the insertion on the
`audit_doc_citations.py` line and put the new entry there — **in the middle of the `GATES` list** —
and labelled its comment `# #29`. That ordinal was already taken by `selftest_git_add_hook.py`. The
result gave one gate **three different numbers**: `#29` in its own comment, `#34` in `04-HANDOFF.md`,
and a third value as its true list position. A Tier 1 reviewer caught it; no gate caught it.

**Root cause — not ignorance of the rule, but not reading it.** `run_gates.py` states the rule
**twice, verbatim, within a few lines of where I typed**:

> ‼‼ APPEND NEW GATES, NEVER INSERT. Gates are cited BY ORDINAL across the docs ('gate #25', 'suite
> #24', 'gate #27'). This entry was first INSERTED at position 4 on 2026-08-17 and silently
> renumbered SIX existing citations; an audit agent caught it.

⇒ **This project had already paid for this exact mistake once, written the warning at the scene, and
I re-committed it anyway.** I chose my insertion point by what made a convenient unique anchor for a
string replacement, and never read the surrounding comment block I was anchoring against.

**The fix.** Moved to the END of `GATES`, renumbered `#34` (the next unused ordinal — the highest
cited was `#33`), reconciled with `04-HANDOFF.md` and `02-ARCHITECTURE.md`, and the entry now carries
its own postmortem so the next person to append reads *why* rather than just *what*.

**Prevention rules.**
1. ⛔ **AN ORDERED LIST WHOSE ELEMENTS ARE CITED BY POSITION IS APPEND-ONLY. Append at the END, and
   take the next UNUSED ordinal — never reuse, never renumber.** Before adding, `grep` the file for
   the ordinal you intend to claim; a collision is silent otherwise.
2. ⛔⛔ **A CONVENIENT STRING ANCHOR IS NOT A CORRECT INSERTION POINT.** When scripting an edit,
   READ the comment block around the anchor before writing — the anchor is chosen for uniqueness,
   which has nothing to do with where the content belongs. *(Every edit in this session used
   anchored replacement; this is the failure mode that technique invites.)*
3. ‼ **AND THE DEEPER ONE: a warning I had not read could not protect me, but a GATE would have.**
   The same session that wrote "anything enforceable belongs in a gate, not in prose" then relied on
   prose. ⇒ a checker for ordinal collisions and mid-list insertion is a real candidate, and until it
   exists this entry is the only thing standing where the last warning already failed twice.


## 2026-09-04 — A GATE PASSED ITS OWN FAULT TEST TWICE WHILE BEING BLIND TO THE DEFECT IT WAS WRITTEN FOR

**Context.** P5 — *"an item's status in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` and the handoff's claim about it move
TOGETHER"* — failed **three times in 2026-09, twice inside the same item**, always as *closing a
CHILD item is not updating the PARENT*. Prose had been tried three times, so per SESSION DISCIPLINE
#6 I wrote a gate: `probe_closed_item_refs.py` (#35), which flags any item describing a CLOSED slug
as still open.

**Symptom.** It reported **`✅ PASS`** on a reconstruction of the genuinely broken file — **twice**,
in two different ways — while its own `inject` fault arm reported **`EXIT=1`** and looked healthy.

**Root cause, both rounds — and both are about the SHAPE of the real text, not the logic:**
1. **Round 1: it matched LINE BY LINE.** The real defect wrapped across three markdown lines — the
   verb *"Add the heal"* on one, *"before building leg 7"* and the slug `#24-ch23healdescent` on the
   next. No single line held both halves. The `inject` arm passed because **I had injected a
   single-line case** — a shape that does not occur in a hand-wrapped 100-column file.
2. **Round 2: it grouped by bullet but matched the RAW text.** `re` `.` does not cross a newline
   without `re.DOTALL`, so `\bADD\b.{0,40}\bbefore\b` still could not span the wrap. Fixed by
   flattening (`" ".join(bullet.split())`) before matching.

**How it was actually caught.** Not by the fault arms — by **pointing the gate at a reconstruction of
the real broken file** (the gate now takes an optional path argument for exactly this). Only then did
it produce the finding it exists to produce, naming the item, the closed slug and the line.

**‼ WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN NO GATE.** A gate that passes for the wrong reason is *load-bearing
false confidence*: it appears in `run_gates.py`, it is cited in the handoff, and every future session
reads its green as evidence. The whole reason this project ratchets gates is so that prose failures
become mechanical — a blind gate converts a known-recurring defect into an *unknown*-recurring one.

**Prevention rules.**
1. ⛔⛔ **A GATE IS NOT PROVEN BY ITS OWN FAULT ARM. It is proven against the ACTUAL DEFECT it was
   written for.** Reconstruct the real broken input — from git history, or by reverting the fix in a
   scratch copy — and require the gate to go RED on it. If the defect is unreconstructable, say so in
   the gate's docstring rather than implying coverage it has never demonstrated.
2. ⛔ **A FAULT ARM MUST REPRODUCE THE REAL SHAPE, NOT A CONVENIENT ONE.** Mine injected one tidy
   line because that was easy to write; the defect lives in wrapped prose. **An arm you can write
   without looking at the real defect is probably not testing it.**
3. ‼ **WHEN A GATE'S FIRST CLEAN RUN IS GREEN, BE SUSPICIOUS, NOT PLEASED** — especially a gate
   written *because* something keeps recurring. #34 went red on its first clean run and that was a
   true finding; #35 went green on a file that was, at that moment, genuinely fixed — which is why
   the reconstruction, not the live file, was the only test that could tell the difference.


## 2026-09-04 — I RETYPED AN ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBER FROM MEMORY AND BAKED THE WRONG ONE INTO PRODUCTION CODE

**Symptom.** Filing `#24-waterfalltimeout`, I wrote that VICTORY_ROAD_B2F "gives **+1428**" frames of
allowance, and Ever Grande "**−2142**". When I later fixed the bug I copied `+1428` **into the
explanatory comment in `walking.py` itself**. A Tier 1 reviewer noticed the same scenario carried two
different values ~13 lines apart in one punch-list item: `+1428` in the old bullet, `+1497` in the
new evidence-sourced one.

**Root cause.** Both original figures were the **un-based terms** — `(map − y) × 42` without the
`195` base — and the B2F one additionally used the **wrong waypoint `y`** (11, the player's, instead
of 14, the waypoint's). The correct values, recomputed from the committed evidence file:
`Ever Grande 195 + (8 − 59) × 42 = −1947` and `B2F 195 + (45 − 14) × 42 = +1497` (right answer `+69`).
`1428` is real but is the **slack**, not the total — which is exactly why it looked plausible.

**‼ WHY THIS ONE STINGS.** It is a wrong number about coordinate arithmetic, written into the comment
of a line whose *entire defect* was coordinate arithmetic, in a codebase that has shipped **three**
backwards index/coordinate fixes. The comment exists to stop the next person getting it wrong, and it
would have taught them a wrong figure. And the evidence file was sitting right there, correct, the
whole time — I retyped from memory of what I had filed hours earlier instead of reading it.

**Prevention rules.**
1. ⛔ **RECOMPUTE AN ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBER FROM THE EVIDENCE AT THE MOMENT YOU WRITE IT.** Never retype
   it from memory of an earlier filing, and never carry it forward from prose into code. If a figure
   is worth putting in a comment it is worth re-deriving in the same minute — this is the same rule
   as *"re-measure a count at the moment you write it"*, which I also broke earlier today with a
   stale line count.
2. ⛔ **THE SAME QUANTITY APPEARING TWICE IS A CHECK, NOT A REDUNDANCY.** When a doc states a value in
   two places, diff them deliberately — a Tier 1 reviewer found this by doing exactly that, and it is
   cheap enough to do while writing.
3. ‼ **A NUMBER THAT "LOOKS RIGHT" IS THE DANGEROUS KIND.** `1428` was a real intermediate from the
   real calculation, so nothing about it read as wrong. Plausibility is not verification.


## 2026-09-04 — I PRICED AN EXPENSIVE REMEDY BEFORE CHECKING THE BOT COULD REACH WHAT IT REQUIRED

**Symptom.** After §Ch23 leg 7 I documented the blocker as *"the party is too degraded for leg 8"*
(35–38% HP, three fainted), filed `#24-ch23attrition`, priced the fix — **up to ~1,073,317 frames,
about five hours of emulator** — and put that decision to the user as the next action. The whole
framing was inverted.

**Root cause.** I never asked whether the bot could **reach** a Poké Center. An observe-only probe
(`--driver ch23retprobe`) then measured, from the B2F landing **B1F (17,16)**: `(8,3)` (leg 6's
ladder to 1F) **UNREACHABLE**, `(30,25)` (back to B2F) **UNREACHABLE**, `(20,21)` (the 1F ladder)
**UNREACHABLE behind the plug**. ⇒ **the bot was TRAPPED on its island. Leg 8 was the only exit**, so
healing, training and shopping were all *impossible* until leg 8 shipped. **Attrition did not block
leg 8; leg 8 blocked attrition.**

**Why it was plausible and therefore dangerous.** Every fact I had was true — the HP curve
(95%→67%→87%→38%) was measured, the training cost was measured, the "no healing inside Victory Road"
finding was decomp-verified. The error was not in any fact but in the **direction of the dependency
between them**, which nothing I had gathered spoke to. ‼ *A correct premise set can still yield an
unactionable plan if you never check the ordering.*

**Cost.** One commit's worth of documentation pointing the next session at the wrong next action, and
a five-hour decision put to the user that they could not have acted on. Caught by my own probe, not
by a reviewer — but only because I happened to ask the reachability question afterwards.

**Prevention rules.**
1. ⛔ **MEASURE THE DEPENDENCY BEFORE PRICING THE REMEDY.** Before quoting a cost — especially one
   measured in hours of the user's time — verify the bot can actually REACH the thing that cost buys.
   A remedy that cannot be applied from the current state is not an option, it is a distraction.
2. ⛔ **WHEN YOU WRITE "X BLOCKS Y", ASK WHETHER Y BLOCKS X.** The two read identically in prose and
   invert the entire plan. This one is cheap to test: ask the planner whether the resources X needs
   are reachable from where the run actually IS.
3. ‼ **AN ESCALATION TO THE USER DESERVES THE SAME EVIDENCE BAR AS A CODE CHANGE.** I would not have
   shipped a fix on an unverified dependency; I should not have shipped a *question* on one either.

## 2026-09-04 — §Ch23 leg 11: "copy the SHAPE from a sibling, but take the CONTRACT from the callee"

**Symptom.** Three consecutive failures opening the League Mart, each one looking like the last fix
should have worked.

**Root cause, and it moved each time.**
1. `NameError: wait_for_no_script_to_run` — the name was imported inside *leg 10's* function body, so
   leg 11's body never had it. **Third time this exact shape has bitten `victory_road.py`** (after
   `os as _os` and `pathlib`).
2. One A-press then `wait_for_no_script_to_run` → *"Cannot buy things in mart because
   `Task_ShopMenu` is not active"*. The clerk has intro dialogue needing several presses, and the
   thing to wait on is a **task**, not the absence of a script.
3. I then copied the target tasks from `buy_poke_balls` — `Task_GoToBuyOrSellMenu` / `Task_BuyMenu` —
   and it STILL failed. Because `buy_poke_balls` **drives the menu by hand and never calls
   `buy_in_shop` at all.** Its shape was right; its tasks were answering a different question.
   `buy_in_shop` checks for **`Task_ShopMenu`** (`higher_level_actions.py:607`).

**The fix that worked.** Poll for `Task_ShopMenu` specifically, bounded at 60 presses, and raise a
message naming the tile and facing if it never opens.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **COPY THE SHAPE FROM A SIBLING, BUT TAKE THE CONTRACT FROM THE CALLEE.** A
neighbouring function shows you the *rhythm* of an interaction; only the function you are actually
calling tells you what state it demands. When a helper fails a precondition, **read that helper**,
not the code that resembles yours.
**Corollary (the deeper one):** a sibling that solves the same problem *a different way* is the most
misleading reference there is — it looks maximally relevant and its details are all wrong. Ask first:
*does this sibling call what I am calling?*

## 2026-09-04 — A success message that was false: backticks inside a double-quoted BASH string

**Symptom.** A one-liner printed `banner updated; 899 lines`, and the gates all passed. The handoff
banner it wrote actually read **`₽56,041 → ₽1,741 ().`** — the fixture name had vanished.

**Root cause.** I embedded Python containing `` `post_league_shop.ss1` `` inside a **double-quoted**
bash string. Bash performed command substitution on the backticks *before* Python ever saw the text,
substituting the (empty, failed) output of running `post_league_shop.ss1` as a command. The only
visible trace was one `command not found` line above an otherwise-successful run.

**Why it nearly shipped.** Every check downstream passed. The assertion passed (it matched text
*around* the hole), the line count printed, `lint_docs` and `audit_doc_consistency` returned 0 —
because **an empty pair of parentheses is perfectly valid Markdown.** Nothing in the toolchain can
see a missing citation; it is only wrong to a reader.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **NEVER PUT BACKTICKS — OR `$` — INSIDE A DOUBLE-QUOTED SHELL STRING.** Write
doc-editing Python to a **file** and run the file; the project already does this everywhere else, and
this is exactly why.
**And the rule that actually caught it:** ‼ **A TOOL'S SUCCESS MESSAGE IS NOT EVIDENCE THE WRITE WAS
CORRECT — READ BACK THE BYTES YOU WROTE.** This is the same lesson as *"'`buy_in_shop` returned' is
not 'the items are in the bag'"*, one layer up, learned twice on the same day: **verify the
CONSEQUENCE, never the call.** A stderr line above a success line deserves to be read before the
success line is believed.

## 2026-09-04 — A `NameError` hiding inside an ERROR MESSAGE, and why eleven passing drives never saw it

**Symptom.** `repro_undefined_names.py` (gate) went red:
`victory_road.py:2274:78: undefined name 'B1F_B2F_APRON'`.

**Root cause.** `descend_to_b2f` derives its apron at run time into a **local** called `apron`
(`apron, step_dir = b1f_ladder_apron()`), but the failure branch's f-string interpolated
**`B1F_B2F_APRON`** — a module constant that has never existed. Almost certainly a leftover from an
earlier draft that used a hardcoded apron, before the derivation replaced it.

**Why every green run missed it, and this is the whole point.** The name appears **only inside the
`raise BotModeError(...)` that fires when the descent FAILS.** Leg 6 has passed on every drive, so
that branch has never executed. ⇒ the bug was **perfectly invisible to testing** and would have
surfaced on the first real failure — replacing *"stepped onto the ladder and did not arrive"*, the
diagnostic written specifically to explain that failure, with a bare `NameError` that explains
nothing. ‼ **The defect would have detonated at exactly the moment it was most needed.**

**The fix.** `{B1F_B2F_APRON}` → `{apron}`, the local the function already computes.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **AN ERROR PATH IS CODE, AND IT IS THE CODE LEAST LIKELY TO BE EXERCISED.**
Every f-string in a `raise` is a live expression: a typo there is a latent crash that testing the
happy path can never find. ⇒ **this is a job for a STATIC gate, not for review or for drives** —
`repro_undefined_names.py` found it in 2.2 seconds after eleven green drives did not.
⭐ **And the more general form, which is the one worth carrying:** *a passing test suite is evidence
about the paths it takes, and says NOTHING about the paths it avoids.* The rarer the branch, the
more it needs a static check — inverted from where attention naturally goes.
‼ Corollary: when a hardcoded constant is replaced by a runtime derivation, **grep for the old
constant's name** before considering the refactor done. This one survived in a string.

## 2026-09-04 — I described the party from MEMORY three times, and every number was wrong

**Symptom.** I briefed a research agent with *"Sceptile L47, Swellow L47, Mightyena L47, Wailord ~L45,
max HP ~115-231"*. The agent built a careful five-fight simulation on it and concluded the run fails
at Drake. Then `probe_ch24_readiness.py` read the actual fixture:

| | I said | **measured** |
|---|---|---|
| Sceptile | L47, 139 HP, 134 Spe | **L53, 147 HP, 160 Spe** |
| Swellow | L47, 129 HP, **138 Spe** | **L48, 139 HP, 129 Spe** |
| Wailord | ~L45, 223 HP | **L47, 226 HP** |
| Mightyena | L47 | **L48** |

**Root cause.** The party had gained levels across eleven legs of Victory Road and I kept quoting the
figures from before the training leg. Nothing forced a re-read, because a party composition *feels*
like something you know.

**Why it mattered more than a typo.** The agent's conclusion turned on exactly the wrong stats:
its argument was *"Glacia's ice OHKOs both mons that outspeed Salamence"* — but **Swellow at 129 Spe
never outsped Salamence's 132 in the first place**, and **Sceptile at 147 HP survives** the 120-142
Blizzard roll that was supposed to kill it. ⇒ **an expensive, well-reasoned analysis was aimed at a
party that does not exist.** The real risk it should have found (one Pokémon, not two, is the entire
speed answer, and it cannot be revived) is *narrower and sharper* than what it reported.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **NEVER DESCRIBE THE PARTY FROM MEMORY — READ THE FIXTURE.**
`probe_anchor_inventory.py <fixture>` prints species/level/HP; `probe_ch24_readiness.py` adds Speed
and the per-item usability verdict. ‼ **And when briefing an agent, PASTE THE PROBE OUTPUT** rather
than paraphrasing it: an agent cannot check the premise you hand it, so **every stat in a brief is a
claim you are making on its behalf**, and its confident conclusion will inherit your stale number
without inheriting your uncertainty about it.
⭐ The general form: *a fact that changes silently as the project progresses is exactly the fact you
will quote from memory.* Party stats, money, item counts and levels are all in that class.

## 2026-09-04 — Quoting a money figure that four weeks of gameplay had moved

**Symptom.** I wrote a decision-log entry budgeting the Elite Four's healing against **₽38,893**, and
planned a basket around it. The live reading at the Mart was **₽56,041** — **₽17,148 more**.

**Root cause.** ₽38,893 was the pre-Victory-Road balance. Victory Road's own trainers paid out on the
way through, and I carried the old figure forward across several documents without re-reading it.

**Why it was nearly costly in both directions.** Under-budgeting would have bought a thinner basket
for a gauntlet that has **no other healing**; and had the drift gone the other way, the leg's own
`LEAGUE_MIN_MONEY` guard would have refused to buy at all. The purchase only matched the plan to the
pokédollar because the code reads `get_player().money` **at run time** rather than trusting the
document.

**The fix that worked.** The leg measures money live and refuses loudly if it is short; the stale
figure was corrected in `04-HANDOFF.md`, `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` and — ‼ **only after a Tier 1 reviewer
caught it** — in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`, which the first two rounds of correction had missed.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **RE-MEASURE A NUMBER AT THE MOMENT YOU SPEND IT**, and have the code read it
rather than the document. ‼ **And when you correct a stale figure, `grep` the whole tree for it** —
this correction reached two of the three current-state files on its first pass, which is the most
dangerous state of all, because the pair check between the two that were fixed returns PASS.
⭐ Distinguish the file kinds while doing it: in an **append-only** file (`06`/`07`/`08`) a dated
later correction is sufficient and the old entry stays; in a **current-state** file (`01`-`05`) the
stale figure must be fixed or annotated **in place**, because nothing tells the reader it is old.

## 2026-09-04 — A field read as if it described itself, twice in one function

Two separate bugs in `#24-e4healing`, both found by DRIVING and neither by a gate, and they are the
same mistake wearing different clothes.

### (a) `parameter` is a UNION TYPE — and Repel's is 100

**Symptom.** The healing plan contained `(4, 'Repel', 'Mightyena at 0/144')`, and the leg died with
*"`Task_HandleChooseMonInput` never became active"*.

**Root cause.** `plan_healing` selected healers with `parameter > 0`. **`Repel`'s parameter is 100 —
one hundred STEPS, not one hundred HP.** A no-target item never opens the party menu, so the run
stalled at a state it could never reach.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **`parameter` MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS FOR DIFFERENT ITEMS** — HP for a potion,
steps for a Repel, 0 for a status cure. **A number cannot identify a category.** Filter medicine by
an explicit allowlist (`ItemFieldUse.Healing`), never by a numeric field being non-zero.
‼ This is the MIRROR of `battle_items.py:85`, which uses the same test to wrongly EXCLUDE Full Heal
and Revive. **One field, read two ways, wrong both times.**

### (b) `field_use` is an ENUM — and comparing it to a string fails silently

**Symptom.** The fix for (a) derived an allowlist with `slot.item.field_use == "healing"`. The next
drive planned the two Revives and the Full Heal correctly and **no HP top-ups at all** — Sceptile
sat at 40/147 and Wailord at 30/226 while the run reported no error.

**Root cause.** `Item.field_use` is an `ItemFieldUse` **enum** (`modules/items.py:92-106`), so the
comparison is always `False` and the allowlist came back **EMPTY**. ⇒ ‼ **It failed silently because
only ONE of the three passes consults the allowlist** — the revive and status passes index the bag
by name directly, so they kept working. **The run looked nearly right.**

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **AN EMPTY FILTER RESULT IS A BUG, NOT A STATE** — `heal_party_from_bag` now
RAISES if the allowlist is empty while the bag holds items. ⭐ And the general form:
**a wrong answer that is a subset of the right answer is far more dangerous than a crash**, because
every surviving part corroborates it. When a change makes output *smaller*, ask what disappeared.

## 2026-09-04 — My fault test found my gate blind: a check whose two arms give the same answer

**Symptom.** Gate #36's most important rule — *revive by battle value, not slot order* — had a
dedicated check, and the check PASSED against a deliberately broken slot-order policy.

**Root cause.** The fixture fainted **Sceptile (slot 0, L53)** and **Zigzagoon (slot 1, L19)**. Sorting
by lowest slot and sorting by highest level **both answer Sceptile.** The two policies were
indistinguishable on that input, so the check could not fail.

**How it was found.** Not by reading it. By breaking the production module four ways in a script and
demanding the gate go red for each — fault A came back `exit=0 ⛔⛔ GATE MISSED IT`.

**The fix.** Both revive checks now put the high-level mon LATER in slot order than a decoy
(Mightyena slot 4 L48 vs Zigzagoon slot 1 L19), so slot order and level order disagree. A fifth
fault arm was added for the Repel bug. All five now fail the gate.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **A CHECK WHOSE ARMS PRODUCE THE SAME ANSWER ON THE CHOSEN FIXTURE IS
VACUOUS, AND IT PASSES LOUDLY.** Before trusting a discriminating check, **compute both arms on that
exact fixture and confirm they differ** — the project already knows this shape (`team_max 39` made a
§Ch21 A/B vacuous), and it recurs because a passing test feels like evidence.
⭐ Corollary, and the reason this is a separate entry from the two above: **a gate is not proven by
its own `--self-test` arm.** #36's built-in self-test was green while the gate was blind. Only
breaking the REAL module proved anything.

## 2026-09-05 — Three of four "worked", and only two were steering

**Symptom.** A moveset leg taught four Pokémon. Three landed on the right move. The fourth
(Zigzagoon, index 1) replaced index 0. Five successive fix attempts — a closed-loop cursor read, a
stability requirement, two task-name corrections and a rewrite — failed to move it, because every
one of them assumed the navigation code was RUNNING.

**Root cause.** `teach_hm_or_tm`'s A-mash loop can blow past the move-selection screen and confirm
the default cursor (index 0). Two of the three "successes" **wanted index 0**, so they were
indistinguishable from the bug.

**What actually found it.** Not reasoning — a **per-iteration trace**. Four teaches produced only
TWO cursor traces; Mightyena and Zigzagoon never entered the navigation block at all.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **A PASSING RESULT FROM A CODE PATH THAT NEVER RAN IS THE MOST CONVINCING
KIND OF WRONG.** When some cases pass and one fails, **prove the passing ones took the path you
think they did** before theorising about the failure. ⭐ The cheap instrument is a trace of the
loop's own reads — not a log of what you passed IN, but of what the code SAW. *(This is the
`#24-instrumenttheaction` rule — "a candidate is not an attempt" — one layer deeper: here the
candidate was right and the code never looked at it.)*

## 2026-09-05 — I sampled a task list once and called it a contract

**Symptom.** After measuring the forget-move screen's active tasks, I concluded upstream's
`Task_HandleReplaceMoveInput` was "the battle path, wrong for the field" and switched to
`Task_HandleInputCantForgetHMsMoves`. My cursor loop then never settled, and the leg refused.

**Root cause.** The screen runs under **both**, at different phases: the "can't forget HMs" task is
**transient** at the start, and `Task_HandleReplaceMoveInput` is the **steady state**. I sampled
once, caught the transient, and generalised. A second trace — over time rather than at an instant —
showed 2 frames of the first task followed by 22 of the second.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **A ONE-FRAME SAMPLE OF A TASK LIST IS NOT A CONTRACT.** Before deciding
what a screen "is", watch it across frames. ‼ And note the shape of the error: **I used a
measurement to overrule working upstream code, and the measurement was the thing that was wrong.**
A single reading is evidence; it is not a contract.

## 2026-09-05 — "Dead slot" was a judgement about purpose, not about numbers

**Symptom.** I twice described Sceptile as carrying *"Rock Smash AND Strength — two dead slots"* and
planned to free both.

**Root cause.** I classified the moves by what they are FOR (field moves) instead of by what they
DO. **`Strength` is 80 BP at 100% accuracy; `Slam` — the move I was keeping — is 80 BP at 75%.**
Strength was Sceptile's *better* Normal move; Slam was the actual waste.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **A FIELD MOVE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEAD SLOT.** Compare the numbers before
calling anything dead. ⭐ More generally: a category label ("HM move", "utility", "filler") is a
hypothesis about value, and the data is one lookup away.

## 2026-09-05 — I invented a new slug for a question the user had already ruled on. Twice-warned.

**Symptom.** Given a new user directive about catching Pokémon and filling the Pokédex, I surveyed
the code, designed a feature, and filed it as **`#24-dexcatch`** with a fresh guard list (ball
reserve, frame budget, PID assertion, owned-set test).

**Root cause.** **`#24-dexhunt` already existed, and the user ruled on it on 2026-07-31.** The
ruling is *"catch every unseen species except when doing so would block progress"*, and it
explicitly PINS the predicate:
> *"'Cheap' is defined, not left to judgement… the codebase already has the right predicate:
> `counter_hunt.resource_blocker()`. **Reuse it rather than writing a second one that can drift.**"*
⇒ **my guard list WAS the second predicate the ruling forbids**, under a slug that forks the record
away from the tracked item. A *second* ruling (`#24-pcoverflow`, 2026-08-05) had already removed the
full-party objection I was designing around — *"A FULL PARTY NO LONGER REFUSES THE CATCH"*.

**How it was caught.** Not by me — by an adversarial reviewer whose first finding was
`06-DECISIONS-LOG.md:1175-1214`. I had read `story_mode.py`, `pokedex.py`, `encounter.py` and
`catch_balls.py`, and measured the dex, the balls and the plateau. **I never grepped the decisions
log.**

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **THIS RULE ALREADY EXISTS AND I BROKE IT ANYWAY** — CLAUDE.md, added
2026-08-23: *"BEFORE ESCALATING ANYTHING TO THE USER, `grep -i` `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` FIRST."* The
first violation cost an escalation about a tracked ROM the user had ruled on five weeks earlier.
This one cost a duplicate design.
⇒ ‼ **THE RULE NEEDS A WIDER TRIGGER, AND THAT IS THE REAL LESSON.** It says *before escalating*. I
was not escalating — I was **designing**, which felt like new work. **A NEW USER DIRECTIVE IS EXACTLY
WHEN THE OLD RULINGS ARE MOST LIKELY TO ALREADY COVER THE GROUND**, because a directive arrives in
the user's language, not in the repo's slugs. ⇒ **grep the decisions log for the TOPIC (`catch`,
`dex`, `pokedex`) at the START of any new feature, not only before escalating.** ⭐ And the tell was
there: `_should_catch` already implemented the exact policy. **Code that already does what you are
about to design is evidence that someone decided this before you.**

## 2026-09-05 — I fixed a pair failure by committing the same pair failure

**Symptom.** A Tier 2 cold-start audit found the `➡➡➡` queue marker naming TWO different "first
actions" with no tie-break, and — worse — ranking first an item whose step 2 could not be started
(*"call the heal BETWEEN ROOMS"* when no rooms exist; `story_mode.py` dispatch stops at Segment 22).
I rewrote the marker. A Tier 2 **RE-audit** then found **four** statements of a first action in the
same file, one of them my fix.

**Root cause.** The order lives in THREE places: the line-10 banner, the 60-second version (line
165), and the marker (line 309). **I rewrote the marker and left the other two** — and both of them
end with the words *"the SAME order as the queue marker"*. ⇒ ⛔ **they falsely certified their own
agreement**, so the cheap consistency check — *does the summary match the queue?* — was answered BY
THE SUMMARY. A reader trusting the 60-second version (which this file calls the first thing a cold
reader sees) would have started the one item that cannot be started.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **A SUMMARY THAT SAYS "the SAME order as X" IS A CLAIM ABOUT X, AND IT GOES
STALE WHEN X MOVES.** Treat every such sentence as another half of the pair and re-read it whenever
the thing it points at is edited. ⭐ And the sharper form: **a cross-reference that ASSERTS agreement
is more dangerous than one that merely restates**, because it disables the check a reader would
otherwise perform.
‼ **THE CONTEXT IS THE POINT: P1 IS THIS PROJECT'S OLDEST NAMED PAIR, AND THE FIX FOR A P1 VIOLATION
WAS ITSELF A P1 VIOLATION.** Knowing a rule, and having just invoked it, does not make you apply it
to your own edit. ⇒ **the re-audit is not optional ceremony** — CLAUDE.md already says *"when a
Tier 2 finding is fixed, re-run Tier 2 and check WHERE the fix landed, not merely THAT it landed"*,
and this is the third time that instruction has earned its keep.

## 2026-09-05 — Three more shapes the same round, all "a fix that landed in one half"

**(a) A COUNT WITHOUT ITS ENUMERATION.** The STATE table's drift cell was corrected from **9** to
**14** — and the list of files underneath was left at **EIGHT**. That cell is *promotion-facing*: a
user ruling taken off it would have promoted 8 of 14. ⇒ ⛔ **A COUNT AND ITS LIST ARE TWO HALVES OF
ONE FACT.** The cell now names `promote.py --check` and refuses to be the authority.

**(b) A LINE-COUNT WRITTEN INTO THE FILE IT COUNTS.** Correcting an inverted budget warning, I
hardcoded *"892/900"* — and my own edit had already made it **893**. The clause it sat in told the
reader to measure rather than repeat. ⇒ ⛔ **A LINE-COUNT IS STALE THE MOMENT IT IS WRITTEN INTO ITS
OWN FILE.** Name the tool, quote no number.

**(c) A PREDICTION PROMOTED TO A FACT BY REWORDING.** The marker read *"It turns DRAKE from a LOSS
into a WIN"*. **The bot has never fought Drake** — §Ch24 is not implemented. Line 165 had it right
(*"analysis says"*); my rewrite dropped the hedge, and the new STATE row repeated the loss of it. ⇒
⛔ **WHEN YOU SHORTEN A CLAIM, THE HEDGE IS THE FIRST THING THAT FALLS OFF, AND IT IS THE PART THAT
WAS DOING THE WORK.** These figures are IV-31/EV-0 estimates, ±15%, with Intimidate unmodelled.

⭐ All four defects passed Tier 0 clean. **`lint_docs`, `audit_doc_consistency` and
`audit_handoff_invariants` cannot see a marker that contradicts the two summaries pointing at it, a
count with a short list beneath it, or a hedge that has been deleted.** ⇒ the mechanical layer bounds
the damage; it does not detect this class. Only a cold reader trying to START does.


## 2026-09-05 — "our data outranks the decomp": right about VALUES, wrong about MECHANISMS

**Symptom.** Four consecutive drives failed to board the Abandoned Ship. Each time I had the correct
coordinates, straight from our own runtime `get_map_data(...).warps`, and each time the bot walked to
the tile and nothing happened.

**Root cause.** I treated a warp TABLE as a route MAP. A warp table gives you a position and a
destination. It does not give you **the warp's KIND** (this one is a NORTH ARROW warp — you stand ON
it and press its own direction), **collision connectivity** (the ship's deck is split in two; the
Captain's Office is not reachable from the boarding tile at all), or **a runtime metatile gate** (the
Storage Room door is stamped `MB_NORMAL` — a WALL — by the map's `OnLoad` until `FLAG_USED_STORAGE_KEY`
is set). Three of the four blockers on this route are invisible in the data I was reading, and I had
explicitly reasoned that our runtime data OUTRANKED a decomp claim to the contrary.

**The fix that worked.** A hand-step experiment: step WEST across (29,6) and print the position. The
bot walked straight THROUGH the tile — which no step-on warp permits — and that single reading
reclassified the problem from "the walk is wrong" to "the warp KIND is wrong". A 7-agent decomp sweep
then found the other three blockers in the same wall-clock time four solo drives had spent finding one.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULE.** **Our data outranks the decomp about VALUES and never about MECHANISMS.** When
a correct coordinate does not work, stop re-checking the coordinate and ask what KIND of thing it is.

## 2026-09-05 — six wrong diagnoses in a row, and the thing I never instrumented was the other half

**Symptom.** Teaching TM13 to Wailord bounces back to the bag with the TM unconsumed. I offered six
causes in sequence — warp-as-waypoint, elevation, aim-at-the-warp, wrong location, party cursor, HM
slot — and every one was plausible, and every one was refuted by the next measurement.

**Root cause (of the wasted effort, not of the bug).** ‼ *(Written before the fix landed and
corrected the same day: this entry originally said the bug was "still open". It was ROOT-CAUSED
and FIXED hours later — see `KI-89` and the entry below. Left visible rather than silently
rewritten, because the sequence is the point: the wasted effort was real before the cause was.)*
Two compounding errors. First, I kept reasoning where I should have been measuring: five of the six
diagnoses were about the PARTY side, and when I finally traced it (`cursor reads=[2,2,2,2,2,2,2,3,3,3]`,
mon under cursor = Wailord) that side proved correct all along. Second — and this is what made it
expensive — **the experiment was bundled inside a 700k-frame ship voyage**, so each wrong guess cost
~12 minutes instead of seconds.

**The fix that worked.** Split the leg at its natural seam. `fetch_ice_beam` is now graded on **TM13
being in the bag**, the fixture `post_icebeam.ss1` is banked, and the teach is its own item iterated
by `--driver ch24teachice` in seconds. ‼ The banked half is a real, complete win; the split is what
made the remaining half cheap to attack.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. **When three diagnoses in a row are wrong, stop diagnosing and start instrumenting** — and
   instrument the half you have NOT yet looked at, not the half you already suspect.
2. **If each attempt is expensive, the first fix is not a better guess — it is making attempts
   cheap.** Bank the part that works, split at the seam, then iterate.

## 2026-09-05 — I wrote the note about `KI-88` in the morning and committed the same bug in the afternoon

**Symptom.** My replacement teach routine, written specifically to avoid the upstream bug, blew past
the move-selection screen and confirmed index 0 — exactly what `KI-88` documents upstream's
`teach_hm_or_tm` doing.

**Root cause.** `KI-88` says *"upstream mashes A and that confirms the cursor's default"*. My own wait
loop pressed A every 4 frames while waiting for the screen. That IS mashing A. I had encoded the
knowledge as a description of someone else's function rather than as a constraint on mine.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULE.** **Documenting a bug does not inoculate you against writing it.** When a note
says "upstream does X and X is wrong", grep YOUR OWN new code for X before you run it — and if the
rule is mechanical, put it in a gate, because prose about a bug has now failed to prevent that exact
bug on the same day it was written.


## 2026-09-05 — the Ice Beam teach: the answer was on screen, in English, for six drives

**Symptom.** Teaching TM13 to Wailord bounced back to the bag, TM unconsumed. Six diagnoses in a row
were wrong (warp-as-waypoint → elevation → aim-at-the-warp → location → party cursor → HM slot).

**Root cause.** Upstream's `scroll_to_item_in_bag` returns SUCCESS with the cursor on the WRONG ITEM
(`KI-89`): asked for TM13 it left it on **HM08 Dive**. Every diagnosis had been about the party menu —
downstream of an item selection that was wrong on the very first frame.

**‼ WHY I DIDN'T FIND IT: I INSTRUMENTED THE INPUT AND CALLED IT THE ACTION.** I *had* added an item
probe. It printed `get_item_bag().tms_hms` — the pocket's CONTENTS — and I recorded "item selection
verified correct: TM13 at pocket index 3". A list of what is in the bag says nothing about where the
cursor is, and the cursor is the only thing A acts on.

**The fix that worked, in one run.** Decode `gStringVar4` — the game's own message buffer — and print
every distinct message before the bounce. It read **`'DIVER already knows DIVE.'`**, naming both the
wrong item and the reason. ‼ Fitted WITH ITS OWN CONTROL: `gStringVar4` is never cleared, so the same
run baselined it on entry (`'NICK put away the TM13…'`) to prove the message had CHANGED — without
that, a stale buffer would have been the seventh wrong diagnosis.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. **BEFORE INFERRING A REFUSAL FROM BEHAVIOUR, READ WHAT THE GAME SAYS — AND BASELINE IT.** A message
   buffer that is never cleared is evidence only when it has CHANGED.
2. **A CANDIDATE IS NOT AN ATTEMPT — and a probe that reads a LIST is a candidate.** If a probe cannot
   fail when the thing it checks is broken, it is decoration. Mine passed every time while the bot
   used the wrong item.
3. **A HELPER THAT HAS WORKED FIVE TIMES IS NOT VERIFIED, ONLY UNMEASURED.** Five earlier teaches
   passed on items whose two index spaces coincide. Prior successes are not coverage.

## 2026-09-05 — I claimed "ARCHIVED VERBATIM" and shipped a truncation

**Symptom.** Tier 1 review caught that two of three punch-list blocks retired to
`28-HANDOFF-ARCHIVE.md` under the words "Full entry ARCHIVED VERBATIM" were truncated — one stopped
mid-sentence — leaving orphaned tails in the punch list under a pointer saying they had been moved.

**Root cause.** An **index-space mismatch**: `hits` was computed against the MUTATED list while
`block_bounds()` scanned the ORIGINAL, so after the first replacement every later block was cut at an
offset from the wrong list. ⛔ This is this project's single most-repeated bug shape — three are filed
against `handle_fainted_pokemon` alone — and I wrote it into a doc script on the same day I was
writing up a different instance of it.

**The fix that worked.** Compute bounds against the same list that is mutated, and — the part that
matters — **assert after writing that every non-blank removed line is present in the archive.** The
first pass made a falsifiable claim with no check behind it. Re-run: 67 lines moved, all verified.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULE.** **A falsifiable claim in a document is worth exactly as much as the check
behind it.** If a script's output asserts "verbatim", "complete", or "all", the script must verify it
before writing — and if it cannot, the claim must be softened rather than the check skipped.


## 2026-09-05 — THE UNIT OF EDIT IS THE CELL, NOT THE SENTENCE (the same error three times in one session)

**Symptom.** Three separate Tier 1 failures in one session, all the same shape:
1. an archive claimed "VERBATIM" while two of three blocks were truncated;
2. two new `###` headers were spliced over an old one and **only the header moved**, leaving ~35
   lines of pre-shipment body under a "CLOSED ⛔ DO NOT REOPEN" heading;
3. a STATE-table cell and an "if stopped mid-task" cell each **contradicted themselves internally** —
   I appended "✅ §Ch23 is WIRED" to the end of cells whose opening clause still read "IS NOT A
   CHAPTER … UNBUILT".

**Root cause.** Every one of my edit scripts substituted **the sentence I had named**. The pair
checks I ran (P1-P5) then passed, because they compare NAMED halves — and the stale text was never
one of the halves I named. ⛔ **A checklist protects exactly what it enumerates**, and I was
enumerating sentences inside units whose OTHER sentences asserted the opposite.

**The fix that worked.** Replace the whole clause, and mark the old wording `*(superseded: …)*` in
place rather than leaving it to be found. For (3), rewrite the cell's opening clause in the same edit
as its closing one.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULE.** **WHEN A FACT CHANGES, THE UNIT OF EDIT IS THE CELL / SECTION / ENTRY, NOT THE
SENTENCE.** A table cell is a claim about everything inside it, exactly as a heading is a claim about
every bullet beneath it (pair P2) — so after changing a fact, RE-READ THE WHOLE CELL from its first
character, not the sentence you replaced. ‼ Corollary, earned by finding (3) twice: **the HOW TO RUN
section is part of every shipped item.** If a command shipped and that section has no line for it, a
cold reader cannot reproduce the item's own evidence — and that section's own text already records
being caught for this once before.


## 2026-09-05 — I committed a root cause that was causally impossible, and it shipped as an instruction

**Symptom.** `KI-90` and its punch-list item were committed and pushed stating that the defect was a
race: *"the target is validated AFTER the A-presses that commit to it, so a faint during move
selection turns a normal turn into a fatal raise."* Two documents then told the next session to build
a repro of exactly that window — **a window that cannot occur.**

**Root cause of the ERROR (not of the bug).** I reasoned from the shape of the code — the check
visibly sits after the A-press loop — and never asked the one question that decides it: **is the
value being checked LIVE or a SNAPSHOT?** It is a snapshot: `_absent_battler_flags` is a plain stored
`int` (`modules/battle_state.py:245`) copied once at `battle_action_selection.py:23`/`:247`. Read
order in the source told me nothing about read TIME.

**The fix that worked.** A 10-agent adversarial workflow: 5 independent angles, each handed to a
separate verifier instructed to REFUTE it. Two were refuted, and the refutations contained the
correction. I then re-verified every load-bearing half myself before touching the docs —
`battle_state.py:396-402`, `battle_state.py:245`/`:821`, `src/battle_util.c:2271`,
`modules/main.py:151-158`, and the 2026-07-22 archived log against `git show -s 72e938d2`.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. **BEFORE BLAMING AN ORDER OF OPERATIONS, ESTABLISH WHETHER THE VALUE IS LIVE OR A SNAPSHOT.** If it
   is a snapshot, "A happens before B" is not a race and any reorder fix is INERT. Source order is not
   evaluation time.
2. **A WRONG ROOT CAUSE IS WORSE THAN NO ROOT CAUSE, BECAUSE IT SHIPS AS AN INSTRUCTION.** A stale
   status wastes a reader's time; a stale instruction spends their day. ⇒ when a diagnosis is
   corrected, GREP THE TREE FOR THE INSTRUCTIONS IT SPAWNED, not just the status sentences.
3. ⛔ **WHEN YOU CORRECT *N* CLAIMS, SWEEP FOR *N* PATTERNS.** I corrected TWO wrong claims here —
   the faint-race mechanism AND the exception-type blast-radius reason — then ran a tree-wide sweep
   for **one** of them. Tier 1 found the other still standing inside `#24-ch23chain`, one paragraph
   above the very NEXT STEP I had just corrected, restating the refuted framing as fact.
   ‼ The sweep was tree-wide and still incomplete, because *breadth of path* is not *breadth of
   pattern*: I had fixed the enumeration failure of scope and kept the enumeration failure of
   subject. ⇒ **list the claims you are retracting, and grep for each one by name.**
4. **THE FIX A WRONG EXPLANATION INVITES IS THE REAL DAMAGE.** Mine invited two: reorder the check
   (inert — the snapshot is frozen), and change the exception type (inert — from a sibling controller
   `BotModeError` sets Manual too). Both would have been "verified" by a run that simply never hit a
   double battle. ⇒ ask what a reader would DO with the explanation, and check that the doing works.

‼ **AND THE METHOD NOTE, because it generalises:** asking a second agent the same question yields a
second guess; asking it to REFUTE yields information. One angle here asserted "this is OUR code, not
upstream" and its own verifier disproved it with an archived log line from three weeks before the
commit it blamed. ⇒ the measured Gemini rule applies unchanged to Claude agents: **grade their
ENUMERATION highly, their CAUSAL CONCLUSIONS not at all.**


## 2026-09-05 — I wrote a repro spec that could not fail, and shipped it as the next session's instruction

**Symptom.** `KI-90`'s corrected entry, the punch-list item and the `➡➡➡` marker all told the next
session to *"stage a DOUBLE battle whose opponent LEFT slot is ABSENT"*. That arm cannot raise:
`story_mode.py:261-313` already returns `use_move_against_right_side_opponent` when the left is absent
and the right is alive. The run would have gone GREEN and been recorded as **"KI-90 does not
reproduce"** — the worst possible outcome, because it retires a real defect.

**Root cause.** I derived the repro from the MECHANISM (`left_battler is None` ⇒ raise) without
checking whether anything upstream of the raise already handles that state. I verified the mechanism
carefully and never asked the next question: **is there a guard between the state and the failure?**
There was — written for this very raise on 2026-07-22.

**The fix that worked.** A scouting agent asked for the cheapest staging computed the discriminator
instead and refuted the premise, quoting the guard. All three live sites now specify the
fall-through condition (left absent **AND** right `hp == 0`), name all three left-hardcoded producers,
and instruct: **print the `TurnAction` the strategy returns before driving anything.**

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔ **A REPRO SPEC IS A CLAIM, AND IT CAN BE VACUOUS.** CLAUDE.md already requires a handed-off A/B
   to have its discriminator computed and its arms shown to differ. **That check belongs on a repro
   the moment it is WRITTEN, not when it is handed off.** Before writing "stage X", find the code
   path between X and the failure and confirm nothing already handles X.
2. ⛔ **A MODULE DOCSTRING IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE MODULE — PAIR P2 APPLIES TO CODE.**
   `victory_road.py` opened with *"LEGS 2 AND 3 ONLY … MUST NOT BE WIRED INTO `_play()` YET"* for ~30
   commits while legs 4-11 and the orchestrator were being written INTO THAT FILE, and it misled a
   subagent on 2026-09-05. Gate #37 enforces this shape for punch-list headings; **nothing enforces it
   in Python**, so when you finish a module, re-read its first ten lines as if you had never seen it.

‼ **AND A THIRD, ABOUT EVIDENCE:** the harness auto-saves stall states into a directory that is BOTH
gitignored AND uses filenames every run reuses (`stalls/repro-ml-fNNNNN.ss1`). The one save capturing
the failing battle was one drive away from being overwritten and could never have reached another
machine. ⇒ **when a run produces evidence you may need again, COPY IT TO A STABLE, TRACKED NAME AND
PIN ITS md5 THE SAME DAY.**


## 2026-09-05 — a guard I could not test, and the one line I keep forgetting to edit

**Symptom (two, same round).** (a) Gate #38's safety guard claimed "raised ANYTHING → the defect is
LIVE" while `drive()` caught only `Exception`; a `SystemExit(0)` from the stub layer produced a
silent **exit 0 with no verdict**, which `run_gates.py` records as a PASS. (b) The `➡➡➡` NEXT ACTION
marker still said "BUILD THE KI-90 REPRO" after the repro shipped as gate #38.

**Root causes.** (a) I wrote the word "anything" and implemented a subset — the same shape as the
message-text guard I had been corrected for one round earlier, so the lesson had not generalised.
(b) I updated FIVE documents and missed the single line the project's own ritual calls authoritative.

**The fixes that worked.** `drive()` now catches `BaseException`; `run_with_verdict_guard()` refuses
to return 0 unless a verdict was printed, which closes the class rather than the instance; the marker
now says the repro is DONE and the live step is the FIX.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (five).**
1. ⛔ **A GUARD THAT SAYS "ANYTHING" BUT EXCLUDES AN EXCEPTION FAMILY IS NOT A GUARD ON ANYTHING.**
   When you write an absolute word in a safety claim, go read the implementation and make it literally
   true — or weaken the word. Both of this gate's holes were absolutes that the code did not deliver.
2. ⛔ **A GUARD YOU CANNOT TEST FROM OUTSIDE IS A GUARD YOU HAVE NOT TESTED.** The first version lived
   inline in `if __name__ == "__main__":`; the fault test could not reach it and reported success
   while exercising nothing. **Put guards in named functions so a test can call them.**
3. ⛔ **WHEN A STEP COMPLETES, EDIT THE `➡➡➡` MARKER FIRST, NOT LAST.** It is the line a cold session
   acts from. Updating five other documents and missing it is not a partial success — the one place
   that drives behaviour was the one place left wrong.
   ‼ ⭐ **A GATE JUDGED ONLY BY ITS RETURN CODE MUST NEVER BE ABLE TO PASS SILENTLY** — that is the
   generalisation worth keeping from this round, and it applies to every gate in the suite.
4. ⛔⛔ **AND THE RULE THAT SUBSUMES ALL OF THEM, EARNED THREE TIMES IN ONE FILE.** I claimed "the
   message check is enough", then "raised ANYTHING", then "the class is closed" — and a reviewer
   refuted each BY CONSTRUCTION, the third by proving a `SystemExit(0)` walked past a `try/finally`
   guard to a silent exit 0. ⇒ ⭐ **STATE A GUARANTEE AS WHAT THE CODE LITERALLY DOES, AND ENUMERATE
   WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER.** Every one of those three was an ABSOLUTE ("enough", "anything",
   "closed") that the implementation did not deliver, and each absolute is a promise the next reader
   relies on. ‼ Mechanically: **`try/finally` OBSERVES a result; only `except` INTERVENES on one that
   never arrives.**
5. ⛔ **A GUARD THAT FAILS THE DOCUMENTED HAPPY PATH TEACHES PEOPLE TO IGNORE IT.**

**‼ AND THE P1 MARKER DEFECT RECURRED A FOURTH TIME ON THIS ONE ITEM — the rule I wrote last round
was not enough.** Last round's rule was *"when a step completes, edit the `➡➡➡` marker FIRST."* I did
exactly that — and the banner (line 10) and the "60-SECOND VERSION (if you read nothing else)" digest
(line 165) still said *"build the KI-90 repro FIRST"*, both of them describing work that had shipped
as gate #38. **The banner's own text promises it lists "the SAME order as the `➡➡➡` NEXT ACTION queue
marker below."**
⇒ ⭐⭐ **A SENTENCE THAT CLAIMS TO MIRROR ANOTHER LINE IS A CLAIM, NOT A DESCRIPTION — AND IT GOES
STALE THE MOMENT THAT LINE MOVES.** Editing the marker first is necessary and NOT sufficient; the
same edit must re-read every sentence that promises to agree with it. The four fast-path readers of
this file (banner, 60-second digest, STATE table, `➡➡➡` marker) are four copies of one fact, and a
cold session may read ANY ONE of them alone — which is precisely why they exist, and precisely why
they are dangerous.
⇒ **The banner now carries that instruction inline**, so the next person to move the marker is told
by the banner itself to come back and fix it. The same guard
   made `--discriminator` — a command in the file's own usage block — always exit 1. That is
   `CLAUDE.md` rule 6's false-positive warning arriving from the other direction: a guard can be
   worthless by being too eager just as easily as by being too lax.


## 2026-09-05 — I invented a project ruling, cited it five times, and let it constrain a real decision

**Symptom.** Five live documents — including the `➡➡➡` marker a cold session acts from — asserted
*"the `KI-83`/`KI-88`/`KI-89` ruling: route around, do not casually patch"*, and I used it to rule out
the most direct fix for `KI-90`.

**Root cause.** KI-89 said "same ruling as KI-88"; KI-88 said the same of KI-83; **nothing at the
bottom of the chain was ever a decision.** I wrote each of those KI lines myself, on different days,
each time believing the previous one was the authority. The premise was also false: `git log` shows
**8** commits to `battle_action_selection.py`, one of them a hang fix in that very file.

**How it was caught.** A decision workflow's PRECEDENT angle was asked to quote the ruling. It could
not find one — and that absence was the finding. I then verified with two commands.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔ **A CITATION CHAIN IS NOT A RULING — FOLLOW IT TO THE ROOT OR DO NOT CITE IT.** If a constraint
   matters enough to decide something, it belongs in `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`, which is where CLAUDE.md
   puts rulings so a question is never answered twice. **"Same ruling as X" is a pointer, not an
   authority**; if X is also a pointer, there is no ruling.
2. ⛔ **A CONSTRAINT THAT FORBIDS SOMETHING YOU HAVE ALREADY DONE IS EVIDENCE THE CONSTRAINT IS
   WRONG.** "Never patch this file" sat in the docs while eight commits had patched it — including
   one I relied on. **Before honouring a prohibition, check whether the tree obeys it.**

⛔⛔ **AND I REPRODUCED THE DEFECT INSIDE THE FIX FOR IT.** Retracting the phantom, I edited the
clause that CITED the ruling and left the ruling's own CONCLUSION — *"route around rather than
casually patch"* — standing as the LAST WORDS of the same sentence. A Tier 1 reviewer found it in the
one file the retraction itself had touched.
⇒ ⭐ **RETRACTING A CLAIM MEANS RETRACTING WHAT IT CONCLUDED, NOT JUST THE SENTENCE THAT CITED IT.**

⛔⛔ **AND THEN I DID IT AGAIN, ONE LEVEL DEEPER — I FIXED THE LEAVES AND LEFT THE ROOT.** The entry
above names the cause exactly: *"KI-89 said 'same ruling as KI-88'; KI-88 said the same of KI-83."*
Those two sentences are the chain. I corrected every entry that CITED the chain — and left both root
sentences standing, unedited, in `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` and `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`. The result: **the same
file asserted "same ruling as KI-88" at line 2889 and "that ruling does not exist" at line 2950**,
61 lines apart. A reader arriving at KI-89 before touching `modules/menuing.py` would have read a
settled authority with no caveat — the precise failure this entry had just diagnosed.
⇒ ⭐⭐ **WHEN YOU DIAGNOSE A ROOT CAUSE, FIX THE ROOT — WRITING THE DIAGNOSIS DOWN IS NOT FIXING IT.**
If your own mistake entry can quote the offending sentences, those sentences are an edit list, not
prose. ‼ This is the SIXTH form of one error in this session — header without its body, marker
without its mirrors, citation without its conclusion, and now diagnosis without its root — every one
of them **"I edited the half I named."**
A citation and its imperative are two halves of one unit, and this project's own "the headline carries
the caveat" rule says the reader reaches the END. **Grep for the CONSEQUENCE, not only the source.**
‼ Note the shape: this is the same "edited the half I named" failure that has now cost this session
five Tier 1 rounds in three different forms — a header without its body, a marker without the
sentences that mirror it, and now a citation without its conclusion.

‼ **And the second-order harm is the one to remember:** the phantom did not merely sit there. It
narrowed a live decision, pushed the analysis toward eight fig-leaf edits at producer sites (one of
them on Teleport, a `target=USER` move where the edit is meaningless), and would have been inherited
by whoever fixed this next. **An invented constraint is more expensive than an invented fact, because
facts get checked and constraints get obeyed.**


## 2026-09-05 — I executed a decision my own log recorded as deliberately undecided

**Symptom.** I wrote the KI-90 fix, verified it, ran the full suite — and an adversarial reviewer
refused to let it land, because `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`'s newest entry (written by me, hours earlier)
says: *"Declare the KI-90 fix approved — rejected, and deliberately… This decision only removes a
FALSE constraint; it does not choose the fix."* No entry choosing it existed. The docs still said
KI-90 was NOT FIXED and `#24-ch23chain` was BLOCKED.

**Root cause.** Removing a false constraint felt like clearing the way to act, so I acted. But the
deferral was a SEPARATE decision with its own carried-forward conditions, and "the obstacle is gone"
is not "the choice is made". ⇒ ⭐ **EXECUTING A DEFERRED DECISION IS ITSELF A DECISION.** It belongs in
the log BEFORE the code lands — which is exactly what CLAUDE.md's Definition of Done step ordering
says (docs 2-4 precede the commit), and what rule 11 exists to enforce.

**A second, smaller error in the same round.** I reported three measured rows as if one command had
produced them; the gate self-retires and returns before two of the three arms run. The values were
true (obtained from separate `capture_target_index()` calls) but the attribution was wrong.
⇒ ⭐ **"MEASURED" MUST NAME THE COMMAND THAT PRODUCED IT** — the sibling of this project's existing
"one trajectory, replayed is not measured twice" rule.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔ **BEFORE WRITING CODE FOR A DEFERRED ITEM, RE-READ THE DEFERRAL AND WRITE THE DECISION FIRST.**
   If the log says "not decided", the first artifact is a decisions-log entry naming the choice and
   the rejected alternatives — not a diff. A deferral carries CONDITIONS; executing without reading
   them back is how a carried finding gets silently dropped.
2. ⛔ **ATTRIBUTE EVERY MEASURED NUMBER TO THE COMMAND THAT PRINTED IT.** If one run does not produce
   the whole table, say which rows came from where — or make one command print them all.

‼ **What went RIGHT and is worth copying:** the reviewer closed a carried-forward objection I could
not (Teleport is `MOVE_TARGET_USER`, and such moves never reach `HandleInputChooseTarget` at all —
`src/battle_controller_player.c:510`), which turned a worry into an argument FOR the layer I had
chosen. **An adversarial reviewer that re-derives the decomp does not only find faults; it can also
supply the evidence you were missing.**


## 2026-09-05 — my completion predicate called a WIPED PARTY "chapter complete"

**Symptom.** The §Ch23 chain drive lost a battle and whited out. The driver printed, on one line:
`AFTER … done=True on_ever_grande=True` next to `ACCEPTANCE: FAIL`. `ch23_chapter_done()` — the gate
`story_mode.py`'s dispatch uses — said the chapter was finished.

**Root cause.** The predicate was `wally_beaten() AND on EVER_GRANDE AND not on a Victory Road floor`.
**A whiteout teleports the bot to the Ever Grande Poké Center**, which satisfies the last two. I built
that predicate specifically to avoid the §Ch15/§Ch18/§Ch19 "passed its own test while stranded" shape
— and it failed from a direction I never considered: not *stranded and claims done*, but **wiped,
teleported to the goal position, and claims done.**

**Why it was worse than stranding.** `StoryMode.run` catches the whiteout's `StoryAbort` and re-enters
`_play()` (`story_mode.py:2392-2426`); the dispatch would then SKIP §Ch23 — including the League heal
and the Elite Four basket, the two legs that exist to survive §Ch24's no-nurse gauntlet. A stranded
bot stops. **This one advances.**

**The fix.** Require the chapter's WORK PRODUCT — the basket — not merely the position. A/B on two
pinned fixtures: the whiteout state flips `True → False`; genuine completion stays `True`.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **A POSITION CAN BE REACHED BY SUCCEEDING *OR* BY FAILING; A WORK PRODUCT CANNOT.** When a
   completion predicate tests WHERE the bot is, ask what ELSE puts it there — respawns, warps, flee
   destinations and whiteouts all move the player without doing the work.
2. ⛔ **THE OBVIOUS EXTRA CONJUNCT WOULD HAVE CHANGED NOTHING.** "Also require a healthy party" is TRUE
   after a whiteout, because whiting out heals you. ⇒ **check that a proposed conjunct is actually
   FALSE in the state you are trying to exclude** — otherwise it is decoration that reads as rigour.
3. ⛔ **A DOCUMENTED DESIGN REASON CAN BE THE THING THAT BUILDS THE HOLE.** My docstring argued, in
   good faith, that consumable conjuncts must be excluded because the predicate could flip back. That
   is true — and it excluded the ONLY conjuncts that distinguish "did the work" from "got wiped and
   respawned at the same place". ⇒ when a rule excludes a whole class of test, ask what the class was
   protecting against before honouring it.

‼ **And the reason this was caught at all:** the drive's own report printed `done=True` beside
`ACCEPTANCE: FAIL` — two verdicts from two different judges on one line. ⇒ ⭐ **PRINT THE THING YOU
GRADE ON *AND* THE THING PRODUCTION GRADES ON; WHERE THEY DISAGREE IS A DEFECT.** Had the driver only
printed its own verdict, this would have shipped.


## 2026-09-05 — I diagnosed a lost battle from the OUTCOME and was about to fix the wrong thing

**Symptom.** The §Ch23 chain drive lost a double battle and whited out. I concluded — and published in
the handoff, the punch list and the changelog — *"that is a levelling/strategy problem, not a defect"*
and *"the wall moved from a BOT DEFECT to a GAME PROBLEM"*, then began researching how to level the
party or avoid the fight.

**Root cause of the misdiagnosis.** I reasoned from the RESULT (it lost a hard fight ⇒ it is too weak)
without ever reading the party state at the moment the fight STARTED. One log line refuted it:
`[BATTLE] started [('Swellow',112,136), ('Zigzagoon',48,48), ('Mightyena',23,143), ('Wailord',0,226),
('Sceptile',0,145), ...]` — **two mons, including the strongest, were already at 0 HP**, after eight
battles with no heal. The party was not underlevelled. It was unhealed.

**What made it a BOT defect after all.** Two healing paths exist and neither runs there:
`heal_party_from_bag()` (`pokemon_league.py:221`) is built and validated but **its only caller is the
harness**; and in-battle items are **unreachable in doubles** because `StoryItemBattleStrategy`
overrides `decide_turn` but not `decide_turn_in_double_battle` (`story_mode.py:417` vs `:261`).

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (four).**
1. ⛔⛔ **DIAGNOSE FROM THE STATE AT THE START OF THE FAILURE, NOT FROM THE OUTCOME.** "It lost" is a
   result, not a cause. The first question for any lost fight is *what did it walk in WITH* — and that
   is one grep of the battle-start line. Losing with a full party and losing with two mons dead are
   different bugs with different fixes, and the outcome line cannot tell them apart.
2. ⛔ **"THE OBVIOUS FIX" IS A HYPOTHESIS WITH A COST.** Grinding levels was plausible, expensive, and
   would have left the defect in place — the party would still enter with its best mons dead, and the
   re-drive would have "proved" that levelling does not help. ⇒ **before building the obvious fix, state
   what the failure would look like if the obvious cause were WRONG**, then check for that first.
3. ⭐ **A CAPABILITY WITH NO CALLER IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY DIAGNOSIS THAT ASKS "CAN WE DO X?"** The answer
   for healing was simultaneously "yes, it is built and validated" and "no, it never runs". ⇒ when
   asking whether the bot CAN do something, always resolve it to **does anything CALL it on this path** —
   and for a class hierarchy, check the *specific method the framework invokes* (`decide_turn` vs
   `decide_turn_in_double_battle`), because an unoverridden method fails SILENTLY by inheritance.
4. ‼ **DO NOT PUBLISH AN INFERENCE IN THE GRAMMAR OF A MEASUREMENT.** I wrote "the leg-9
   Katelynn+Quincy double" as fact; the trainers were never named in any log. It happened to be
   RIGHT — pos=(31,17) sits on the bridge between them — but I only learned that afterwards, and a
   reviewer could not have told my inference from my measurements. ⇒ **name the source in the sentence**,
   or mark it as inferred until it is checked.

‼ **And the reason this was caught:** an agent I had sent to fetch party data reported that the trainer
names appeared in NO log. That was half-wrong (they are in the map recon, not the logs) — but chasing
the half that was right is what made me open the drive log at all. ⇒ ⭐ **A PARTIALLY-WRONG REPORT THAT
CONTRADICTS YOUR ASSUMPTION IS STILL WORTH OPENING THE FILE OVER.** Do not dismiss the whole report
because part of it is refutable.


## 2026-09-05 — right diagnosis, WRONG PRESCRIPTION: I proposed a fix this chapter had already tried and rejected

**Symptom.** Having correctly measured that the leg-9 loss is ATTRITION (the bot entered with two mons
at 0 HP), I specified the fix as *"wire `heal_party_from_bag()` into the leg-9 approach"* and wrote it
into the punch list, the handoff banner, the 60-second digest and the `➡➡➡` marker — four places.

**Root cause.** I went from *diagnosis* straight to *remedy* without asking whether this project had
already solved the same problem. It had — **twice**, both closed and both A/B-proven, and both sitting
in the same file I was editing:
* `#24-ch23healdescent` — `heal_before_descent()` heals at a **Poké Center** via the 1F south
  arrow-warp. A/B: **un-healed 32% / 3 fainted → healed 87% / 0**.
* `#24-ch23attrition` — `heal_at_league`, a 36-step walk to the League Center: **36/807 with five
  fainted → 807/807 with none**. ‼ It also states outright that **there is NOWHERE to heal inside
  Victory Road**, and that leg 6's heal works *only* because it runs from 1F, one warp from the door.

**And the closed items contained the number that REFUTES my prescription:** `#24-ch23attrition` records
the wallet **spent down to ₽1,741** with **ONE Potion** in the bag by leg 11. ⇒ **bag-healing at leg 9
would have had almost nothing to spend.** I would have built it, driven it, and measured "no
improvement" — and the natural reading of that result is *"healing doesn't help, so it IS a levels
problem"*, which would have sent the next session back to the grinding idea I had just ruled out.

**The correct remedy, which the same items hand over for free:** the fatal fight is on **1F at (31,17)**
— architecturally the *same* position leg 6 heals from. ⇒ apply the **proven** mechanism a second time,
rather than introducing a new one.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **A DIAGNOSIS AND A PRESCRIPTION ARE TWO SEPARATE CLAIMS, AND EACH NEEDS ITS OWN EVIDENCE.**
   Being right about the cause creates confidence that silently carries into the cure, where it was
   never earned. ⇒ after naming a cause, **stop and ask separately: has this project already fixed
   this, and what did it learn?**
2. ⛔ **BEFORE PRESCRIBING A MECHANISM, GREP FOR THE *PROBLEM*, NOT THE SLUG.** I searched for
   `#24-ch23chain`'s own text and found its halves. The two items that mattered were named
   `#24-ch23attrition` and `#24-ch23healdescent` — they would have surfaced on `attrition` or `heal`,
   words from **the diagnosis**, which is what I had and did not use.
3. ⭐ **A CLOSED ITEM IS THE CHEAPEST RESEARCH IN THE TREE, AND IT CARRIES NUMBERS A FRESH AGENT
   CANNOT GET.** Neither the decomp agent nor the code agent could have told me the bag holds one
   Potion and ₽1,741 — that is *our run's* history, and it is the fact that decides between the two
   candidate fixes. ⇒ **read the closed neighbours of an open item before speccing it**, and note that
   this is exactly what `03`'s 90 completed `[x]` items are FOR.

‼ **Sequence worth preserving:** an agent's partly-wrong report made me open the drive log (finding
the real cause); the drive log made me respec the item; respeccing pushed the file over its line
budget; the budget forced me to list closed blocks — **and the listing is what revealed the two prior
fixes.** ⇒ ⭐ **The line-budget gate did real diagnostic work today that it was never written to do.**
That is an argument for keeping cheap mechanical constraints even when they feel like bureaucracy.


## 2026-09-05 — I wrote the correction and left the refuted sentence DIRECTLY AFTER IT (9th instance)

**Symptom.** Having measured that the leg-9 loss is attrition, I inserted the corrected reasoning into
the handoff banner. A Tier 1 reviewer then found the banner reading, in a single paragraph:

> "⛔ **DO NOT GRIND — levelling would not have fixed this**; the party would still walk in with its two
> best mons dead. ⇒ **the wall moved from a BOT DEFECT to a GAME PROBLEM** (levelling/strategy), which
> is the next question."

**Two adjacent clauses of one sentence flatly contradicting each other** — in the file a cold session
reads first, at three sites, plus two more in the punch list and one in a research-note stub. Six live
sites total.

**Root cause — the same one, for the ninth time in this session: I edited the half I named.** I had a
list of "the sites that state the next action" and swept exactly those. The refuted CONCLUSION was a
different sentence, three words later, and it was never on my list. ⛔ **Adjacency made it worse, not
better:** because my correct text was right there, I read the paragraph as fixed.

**⭐⭐ THE VALUABLE PART — WHICH CONTROL CAUGHT IT, AND WHICH ONE COULD NOT.**
Earlier the same day I wrote a mechanical gate for exactly this failure class, found it false-positived
on its first live run, and deleted it (`06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` 2026-09-05), recording that the class was
