reached for the most physically plausible story — *it must be fainting* — and then wrote that story
down **with a fabricated statistic attached to make it look measured**. The `42 of 47` is the tell: a
precise-looking ratio invents authority that a hedge ("it was probably fainting") would not have.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A NUMBER IN A DOC MUST BE TRACEABLE TO A COMMAND. Before writing any figure,
be able to name the exact grep/script that produced it, and prefer PASTING that output to
paraphrasing it.** If the number came from reading rather than running, it is an impression and must
be written as one: *"the log looks like it is fainting"* is honest; *"0/43 HP in 42 of 47 readings"*
is a claim of measurement. ‼ This project already requires raw output for GATE results; the same bar
must apply to any statistic that enters a doc or a comment.

**⛔ WHY IT WAS EXPENSIVE, and it is not the wrong sentence.** The invented figure became the sole
support for a general principle — *"the frame ceiling is a PROXY FOR SURVIVABILITY"* — which was then
used to justify leaving a guard alone and to close off a line of investigation. **A fabricated
datum does not stay local; it gets promoted into a rule.** Withdrawing it reopened a question that
had been treated as settled for a day.

**⭐ What saved it from being worse:** the underlying observation was real and independently
recomputable — 69 battles was ~22x enough for a level, so "gained nothing" genuinely did prove
near-zero participation. ⇒ **separate the OBSERVATION from the EXPLANATION when writing.** Had I
recorded only "69 battles, zero levels, cause unknown", everything downstream would still have been
true and nothing would have needed withdrawing.

**‼ And the specific trap that made the wrong explanation so believable: I never checked whether the
feature I was reasoning about was even RUNNING.** The driver returned a different battle strategy
entirely, so swap-training never executed — 232 turn decisions, 0 rotations. ⇒ **before explaining
why a mechanism behaved badly, prove it EXECUTED.** One log line naming the strategy class would have
ended a day of wrong reasoning, and it is now the first vacuity gate on the test spec.

## 2026-09-09 — I broke my own new rule inside the commit that created it

**Symptom.** I wrote a prevention rule — *"a number in a doc must be traceable to a command"* — and in
the same commit published four documents containing statistics I had never run a command to obtain. A
Tier 1 reviewer found one of them (*"exp1757 constant across 771/771 harness snapshots"*) unlocatable:
the string is not in that log at all; it lives in 73 other files. I had mis-attributed another run's
measurement. The reviewer also found the commit's CENTRAL claim false: I said `0/43` appeared
*nowhere*, and it appears **53 times**.

**Root cause.** A six-agent investigation returned a dense, confident, well-cited report. I adopted
its numbers wholesale because it had *earned* credibility on the part I could check (the mechanism
finding was airtight, and I verified that one). **Credibility on a verified claim does not transfer to
the unverified ones in the same report.** `CLAUDE.md` states the rule outright — *"their output is a
NOTE, never truth"* — and I had even quoted it earlier the same day.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — VERIFY EVERY NUMBER YOU REPUBLISH, NOT EVERY REPORT.** Trust is per-CLAIM, not
per-SOURCE. When adopting a subagent's findings, split them into (a) claims I re-ran myself, which may
be stated flatly, and (b) claims I did not, which must be attributed *in the text* — "an agent
measured X" — or dropped. ‼ The cost of the shortcut here was a THIRD false statement about the same
47 lines of log, and a reviewer's whole cycle spent catching it.

**‼ AND THE STRUCTURAL LESSON, which is the transferable one: A CORRECTION IS A HIGH-RISK EDIT.**
Both times I corrected this claim I made it worse, because the correcting frame ("I was wrong, here is
the truth") carries an authority the evidence had not earned. ⇒ **hold a correction to a HIGHER
evidentiary bar than the original claim, not a lower one** — the reader has already been misled once
and has no reason left to be sceptical on my behalf. Concretely: for a correction, paste the raw
command output INTO the document rather than paraphrasing it, so the next reader can re-run it without
trusting me at all. That is what round 3 does.

**⭐ What finally worked:** running two throwaway scripts (`verify_marill.py`, `verify_envelope.py`)
and pasting their output verbatim. Ten minutes, and it also independently reproduced the swap-training
envelope (max observed gap +6 across 24,244 decisions) that the user's catching/bench design depends
on — turning advice I had given on trust into advice I can defend.

## 2026-09-09 — A parser that loses ROWS inflates every RATE, and announces nothing

**Symptom.** Turning a scratch measurement into a checked-in tool, I "tightened" its regex. The tool
then reported the swap-training rotation rate at gap +2 as **62.3%**. The scratch version had said
**29.9%**. Both looked entirely plausible.

**Root cause.** The stricter pattern required the logged action to be followed by exactly one space
and `vs`. Real lines log moves as `UseMove:Water Spout(pp5)`, so spacing varies — and the tighter
regex silently dropped **two thirds of the denominators** (24,244 decisions became 7,671) while
capturing **every single numerator** (10, 2, 713, 192, 56, 24, 5 — identical in both). Losing only
the rows where nothing happened doubles or triples every rate.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN A PARSER CHANGES, COMPARE ITS DENOMINATOR, NOT ITS ANSWER.** A rate is a
ratio, and a filter that drops non-events moves it hard while every headline number it reports still
"looks about right". ⇒ any edit to an extraction pattern must print **total rows matched** before and
after, and a drop is a defect until explained. ‼ Numerators agreeing is NOT reassurance here — it is
the signature of exactly this bug, because the rows being lost are the boring ones.

**‼ What caught it:** the new tool was required to REPRODUCE a table that had already been published.
It did not, and the mismatch was visible in one line. ⇒ **when converting a throwaway measurement into
a durable tool, make reproducing the original output the acceptance test** — otherwise the rewrite is
a new, unvalidated instrument wearing the old one's credibility. An independent re-implementation by a
reviewer landed within ~1% of the permissive counts, which is what settled which version was right.

**⭐ And the reason the tool exists at all is worth keeping:** a reviewer could not reproduce a figure
because the script that produced it lived in a scratch directory. A number whose command is not in the
repo cannot satisfy this file's own rule that a reader should be able to re-run it "without trusting
me at all". ⇒ **if a measurement is worth publishing, its script is worth checking in.**

## 2026-09-09 — My retracted claim propagated INTO the next investigation and nearly corrupted a second doc

**Symptom.** I launched a five-angle investigation whose brief included my own (wrong) correction that
a `0/43` HP figure had been *fabricated*. Three of the five angles duly reported that the punch list
"carries a fabricated statistic" and recommended editing it out. The adjudicator measured instead of
trusting, found **51 genuine zero-HP readings**, and wrote: *"Do not action the 'punch-list carries a
fabricated 0/43' doc fix — it is wrong."*

**Root cause.** A brief is not neutral. Everything I assert in it is inherited by every agent as
established fact, *with my confidence attached and none of my doubts*. My error had a one-hop
multiplier: one wrong sentence in a prompt became three agents recommending a destructive edit.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — LABEL EVERY CLAIM IN AN AGENT BRIEF AS *MEASURED* OR *BELIEVED*, AND INVITE
REFUTATION OF THE BELIEVED ONES.** This project already tells agents what is RULED OUT so they do not
re-derive it; the missing half is telling them **which of my "facts" are load-bearing but unverified**.
⇒ a brief should carry an explicit line: *"the following are my beliefs, not measurements — check them
first and say so if they are wrong."* The adjudicator did that unprompted and it is the only reason
this was caught.

**‼ AND THE STRUCTURAL POINT: A RETRACTION MUST CHASE ITS CITATIONS.** When I retracted the fabricated
figure I fixed the four documents. I did not think about the investigation that was ALREADY RUNNING on
a brief containing it. ⇒ **when you retract something, ask what is in flight that was built on it** —
a correction that does not reach the work already downstream of the error is only half a correction.

**⭐ What worked, and is worth copying:** the adjudicator was instructed that "agreement between agents
is NOT evidence" and that it must verify load-bearing claims itself. It did, against three agents
saying the same wrong thing. **Majority agreement among agents fed the same brief measures the brief,
not the world.**

## 2026-09-09 — FOURTH re-discovery in one session. The rule I keep writing does not fire; here is one that can.

**The four.** Each was presented as a new finding and each was already in this tree:

| # | I "found" | already at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the B1F training ground is richer | `07-CHANGELOG.md`, refuted **the same morning** |
| 2 | there is no team training after Winona | `#24-regimeb-noescalation`, same 8-and-8 count |
| 3 | stale drift claims | an audit had listed three; I treated the list as the population |
| 4 | the estimator understates trainee cost ~2x | `03-PUNCH-LIST.md:3747`, filed **one day earlier, same file** |

**Why "grep the docs first" keeps failing.** It is a rule about *diligence*, and diligence is exactly
what is missing at the moment of discovery: finding something feels like the end of a search, not the
start of one. Three times I wrote the rule down and three times the next finding walked straight past
it — because the rule names no ACTION, only an intention.

**⭐⭐ THE MECHANICAL VERSION, which is checkable in ten seconds:** before writing a finding down,
**pull the two or three most distinctive NOUNS out of your own sentence and grep `PROJECT KNOWLEDGE`
for each.** Not "search the docs" — grep `estimator`, grep `Winona`, grep `B1F`, grep `drift`. Every
one of the four above would have returned its own prior filing on the first term. ⇒ **the finding's
own vocabulary is the query; you do not have to know what to look for.**

**‼ AND THE HALF THAT REDEEMS IT, which is worth as much as the rule.** On #4 the reviewer that caught
the duplication also identified what WAS genuinely new, and it was better than my claim: the prior
entry ended *"any future costing of a catch-time top-up must double the estimate"* — and the item's
own FIX DIRECTION two bullets later never did, still pricing at full XP. ⇒ **a re-discovery is not
worthless; it is a signal that a known fact was never APPLIED.** When you find you have re-derived
something, do not just cross-reference and move on — **ask what the original filing told the project
to do, and check whether anything did it.** That question turned an embarrassing duplicate into the
actual defect: the item instructed itself to double and then didn't, so its planned fix would have
failed for a reason it had already written down.

## 2026-09-09 — My retraction reached the changelog and the code, but not the two files agents read first

**Symptom.** I fabricated a statistic on 2026-09-08, retracted it twice on 2026-09-09, and it was
**still live** in `04-HANDOFF.md` when a six-agent investigation launched today — which duly
re-derived a killed argument from it. The adjudicator found it and told me to fix the docs before
anything else.

**Root cause, and it is precise.** `04-HANDOFF.md:375` is a **3,000-character line** that mentions the
survivability conclusion TWICE. My annotation landed on the second mention; the first — the one
carrying the invented "42 of 47" — was never touched. A `grep` for the CONCLUSION found a hit and I
stopped, because a hit that is already annotated looks like a job done.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN RETRACTING, GREP FOR THE *EVIDENCE* AND FIX *EVERY* OCCURRENCE, THEN
RE-GREP AND REQUIRE ZERO UNANNOTATED HITS.** Do not grep for the conclusion; grep for the NUMBER. A
fabricated figure is a distinctive string ("42 of 47") and appears exactly where it did damage,
whereas a conclusion is paraphrased and hides. ⇒ the check is mechanical: after the fix, every
occurrence must have a withdrawal marker within a few hundred characters, and that is assertable in
one loop — which is how I finally verified it.

**‼ AND THE COST, which is the part worth internalising: an incomplete retraction is not neutral, it
is an ACTIVE trap.** The stale line sat in the file every agent opens first, so it was not merely
unhelpful — it seeded the next investigation's premise, and five of six agents inherited it. The
adjudicator caught it only because it was told that agreement between agents is not evidence.
⇒ **a retraction is finished when the ERROR cannot be re-read as current, not when the correction has
been written.**

**⭐ Corollary for long lines, which this tree is full of:** annotating "the" occurrence is meaningless
in a file whose lines run to thousands of characters and repeat their claims. Count the occurrences
first; if there is more than one, annotate them all or rewrite the line.

## 2026-09-09 — THIRD time republishing an agent's statistics unverified. The rule exists; here is a gate-shaped replacement.

**Symptom.** A reviewer refused a block of figures ("median burn 86%, spare 707,123, 9 of 16 over
budget") because nothing in the repo produced them. It was right: I had lifted them from an
adjudicator's report and written them into a current-state file **two commits after writing the rule
"trust is per-CLAIM, not per-SOURCE."**

**What re-measuring found.** Two figures reproduced (85.8% vs 86%, 710,600 vs 707,123). **Three did
not** — median battlers-under-target **3.5 → 3.0**, and the over-budget counts **9/16 → 10/16** and
**13/16 → 14/16**. Small, and that is the point: *"close enough"* is the same permission that produced
the original fabrication. A number I cannot reproduce is a number I may not publish, however plausible.

**Why the existing rule keeps failing.** "Verify what you republish" is a *disposition*, and it is
competing with a report that is dense, well-cited, and right about everything I DID check. Verifying
the checkable parts creates a feeling of having verified the report. It has not.

**⭐⭐ THE MECHANICAL REPLACEMENT — a statistic may enter a document by exactly THREE routes, and
there is no fourth:**
  1. **PASTED OUTPUT** of a command shown beside it; or
  2. **A CITATION TO A CHECKED-IN TOOL** that reproduces it (`probe_swaptrain_envelope.py`,
     `probe_ch23_headroom.py` — both exist because of this failure); or
  3. **EXPLICIT ATTRIBUTION IN THE TEXT** — *"an agent measured X; I have not reproduced it."*
⇒ If a figure fits none of the three, DELETE IT. ‼ This is checkable by a reader in seconds, which a
disposition never is — and it is why route 2 has now caught two different errors that route 0
(silently adopting) shipped.

**‼ AND THE ASYMMETRY WORTH REMEMBERING: the reviewer that refused these numbers was WRONG about the
headline** — its 3-run spot-check suggested ~67%, and the full 16-run measurement confirmed 85.8%. It
was still right to refuse, because its objection was not "your number is wrong" but "your number has
no command." ⇒ **a demand for provenance is correct even when the figure turns out to be true**, and
answering it produced a reusable tool plus three corrections. Do not argue with that objection; run
the command.

## 2026-09-09 — I put two WRONG "MEASURED" claims into an agent brief, and labelling them did not save me

**Symptom.** I had just adopted the rule *"label every claim in a brief as MEASURED or BELIEVED"*, and
did so. Two of the things I labelled **MEASURED** were wrong:
  * *"`best_training_grass` has ZERO call sites"* — it is imported and called by
    `tools/story-dev/repro_no_return_grounds.py`. My grep had been scoped to `sandbox-pokebot/` and
    `PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/`, so `tools/` was invisible to it.
  * *"`_prepare_for_fight` relocates only when `local_max + FODDER_LEVEL_GAP < team_max`"* — that is
    the LEGACY branch; `FODDER_RULE` has defaulted to `"xp_rate"` since a later change. I took it from
    `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`, which was accurate when written.

**Root cause.** Labelling protects a reader from a claim I KNOW is soft. It does nothing for a claim I
believe *because I once ran a command whose scope I have forgotten*. The first was a **stale
measurement** — right when taken, wrong now; the second was a **narrow measurement** presented as a
general one.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A "MEASURED" LABEL MUST CARRY ITS SCOPE AND ITS DATE, OR IT IS NOT A
MEASUREMENT.** Write *"zero call sites in `sandbox-pokebot/` as of today"*, not *"zero call sites"*.
The scope is where staleness and over-generalisation both hide, and it costs four words. ⇒ when
re-using a figure from a decisions log or an older entry, **re-run it or date it** — a decisions log
records what was true when the decision was made, which is exactly the wrong thing to quote as
current.

**‼ WHAT WORKED, and is the reason to keep briefing this way:** because the claims were labelled at
all, three angles knew they were allowed to contradict me and did — flagging both errors explicitly
rather than building on them. **A brief that invites refutation gets refuted; one that asserts gets
obeyed.** The labelling was not sufficient, but it was load-bearing.

## 2026-09-09 — Two totals matching is not pairing (and I made the substring mistake twice in one round)

**Symptom.** *"Does a training relocation deliver battles?"* got four answers. Three were wrong:
| # | answer | why it was wrong |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | agent: 114 relocations / 114 drops, **1:1, zero battles delivered** | aggregate totals, no pairing |
| 2 | me: **128 not 114**, so "not established" | contaminated grep — 14 counter-hunt lines that merely NAME the map |
| 3 | reviewer: anchored count is **exactly 114**, so the 1:1 **holds** | correct about my contamination, still aggregate |
| 4 | per-run pairing: **252 delivered / 130 dropped / 71 unknown** | the actual answer |

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — AN AGGREGATE CANNOT ATTRIBUTE. If a claim is of the form "X causes Y", count
(X,Y) PAIRS WITHIN THE SAME UNIT, never totals of X and totals of Y.** Two equal totals feel like
proof and are not: 114-vs-114 read as certainty, 453-vs-613 read as nothing, and both hid the same
28.7% failure rate. ⇒ **matching totals are the weakest possible evidence for causation and the most
persuasive-looking.**

**‼ AND THE HUMBLING PART: I made the substring-is-not-a-message error TWICE IN ONE INVESTIGATION** —
once with a regex that captured `S` from `Story:`, then again with a filter that swept in a different
subsystem's failures because both mentioned the same map name. I had written the rule up between the
two. ⇒ the durable fix was not another rule but a CHECKED-IN TOOL that (a) anchors on the full message
shape and (b) **prints the look-alike it excludes**, so the filter is auditable instead of trusted.
**When a question has produced more than two conflicting answers, stop answering it and build the
instrument** — the third grep is not more likely to be right than the first two.

## 2026-09-09 — "I cannot verify this" is a finding, and it pointed at a better deliverable than the one I was chasing

**Symptom.** I set out to verify a figure I had published as `[AGENT, UNVERIFIED]` — *"88.8% of
laggards are already behind when first seen"* — because it was the justification for choosing what
to work on next. I could not reproduce it. The instinct was to try harder or to accept the number.

**What the failure actually meant.** The data could not support the question **at all**: party
telemetry records `Species:L<level>` and nothing stable, so no Pokémon can be followed across
readings. `Species#PID` existed in 96 lines, all of them one error message. ⇒ the claim was not
merely unverified, it was **unverifiable with current instrumentation** — and so was a *second*,
unrelated question that had stalled days earlier for what looked like a different reason.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN A NUMBER CANNOT BE REPRODUCED, ASK WHETHER THE DATA COULD PRODUCE IT AT
ALL BEFORE ASKING WHETHER IT IS TRUE.** A failed reproduction has two very different causes: the
claim is wrong, or the measurement was never possible. They call for opposite responses — argue with
the claim, or **build the instrument**. ⇒ check the SCHEMA before re-running the query.
‼ And the payoff for asking: two blocked investigations turned out to share one missing field. **A
gap that blocks two unrelated questions is not a side quest; it is the highest-value thing on the
board** — and it was invisible while each question was treated on its own.

**⭐ The shape of the fix is worth copying too.** The obvious move was to add identity to the existing
`party_key`. That key drives event detection, so enriching it would have silently changed which
frames count as a catch or a level-up — a behaviour change disguised as telemetry. **Adding a
SEPARATE field that nothing reads costs one line and cannot regress anything.** When instrumenting,
prefer a new field over enriching a load-bearing one.

### 2026-09-09 (same day, caught by review) — I cited two green gates as validating a file neither gate reads

**Symptom.** Shipping a new `except Exception` in `modules/debug_logger.py`, I listed
`repro_no_silent_except.py` and `repro_undefined_names.py` among the gates that passed, and let that
stand as evidence the handler was acceptable. Both **do** pass. **Neither scans that file** —
`repro_no_silent_except.py`'s budgets cover `modules/story`, `modules/battle_strategies`,
`modules/battle_action_selection.py` and `modules/modes/util`; `debug_logger.py` is not in `BUDGETS`
at all, and `repro_undefined_names.py`'s scope is `modules/story` + `plugins/custom_modes` +
`story_harness.py`. The green was true and **irrelevant**.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A GREEN GATE IS EVIDENCE ONLY ABOUT THE FILES IT ACTUALLY READS. Before
citing a gate as validation, read its SCOPE/BUDGETS and confirm the file under test is in it.** This
trap is nastier than a broken gate: a broken gate eventually fails on something, whereas an
out-of-scope gate passes *identically* whether the code is clean or catastrophic. ⇒ **"the gates are
green" is not a safety argument for a file outside them** — the argument has to be the code, read
directly. *(Here it holds: `None` slots skipped, unreadable PID degraded, per-mon `except`, and the
whole call wrapped again by `_safe()`. That is a real property; it just was not gate-certified, and
saying so is the difference between an argument and a rubber stamp.)*

**‼ AND A SECOND, SMALLER ONE FROM THE SAME REVIEW: a scope note has to be TRUE, not merely present.**
I labelled a measurement *"`*.log` only"* when the figure came from `stdout.txt`. The project rule was
already *"a MEASURED claim must carry its SCOPE"* — I carried one and it was wrong, which is worse
than none, because a stated scope is the thing a future reader uses to reproduce. ⇒ **paste the scope
from the command you ran, never from memory of what you meant to run.**

## 2026-09-09 — "Copy the pattern that worked" is not a cost argument (and a spec's symbol was invented)

**Symptom (avoided, not suffered).** Having just shipped `party_ids` — collected in `_light_state`,
which runs **every frame** — I was about to add dex telemetry the same way. Pricing it first showed
the two are not comparable: `party_ids` is free because `_party_exp` **already** walks the party every
frame, whereas `Pokedex.owned_species` (`modules/pokedex.py:42-52`) loops **412 indices** building a
`Species` per hit, with `get_pokedex()` re-reading on a stale cache. ⇒ the copy would have put a
412-iteration scan on the hot path.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — TWO FIELDS THAT LOOK IDENTICAL IN THE LOG CAN DIFFER BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE IN
WHAT THEY COST TO PRODUCE. Price the READ, never the output line.** The tell is not the shape of the
value but whether the surrounding code was *already* paying for it. ⇒ the dex read went in the
**heartbeat** (~1/minute), and its docstring says why it must never move.

**‼ SEPARATELY, FROM THE SAME ITEM: a design spec named a function that does not exist.**
It fenced the new path with `counter_hunt.hunt_active()`; the tree has **zero** mentions — the real
name is `is_armed()`. The cited *line number was right*, which is exactly what makes this shape
dangerous: precise-looking citation, invented symbol. ⛔ And it would have failed **silently**,
because the call site wraps everything in `except Exception: return False` ⇒ feature never fires,
A/B reports "no difference", and the result reads as a **refutation of a feature that never ran**.
**⭐ RULE: before implementing any spec, grep EVERY symbol it names — a spec is a claim, and a symbol
name is the cheapest possible claim to check.** *(One invented in six here.)* This generalises the
existing "grade the NAMES highly and the ARCHITECTURE ADVICE not at all" rule from Gemini to **any**
agent output, including a multi-agent adversarial pass that had already refuted its own weakest
angles.

**‼ AND A THIRD, ABOUT MY OWN INSTRUMENT.** To check the pass's run-end frequencies I grepped for
phrase PRESENCE per run segment and got wildly different numbers (79.6% vs 32.7%) — then realised I
was measuring *"does this phrase appear anywhere"* while they measured *"what ENDED the run"*.
`is fodder for a L18 team` is a mid-run relocation message, not a terminal cause. **Neither number
refutes the other; they are different questions.** ⇒ **PRESENCE CANNOT ATTRIBUTE A TERMINAL CAUSE** —
the same "an aggregate cannot attribute" error wearing a new costume, and I nearly published it as a
contradiction. *(What did validate: my segment counts, 53 and 49, matched theirs exactly ⇒ same
corpus, same boundaries, so the divergence was purely presence-vs-cause.)*

## 2026-09-09 — Five green test arms, none of which called the function under test

**Symptom.** I added dex telemetry, proved it with a stub suite, and shipped. Five arms passed:
correct dex set, correct delta wording, an unreadable dex degrading to `owned=?`, a shrinking set
emitting nothing, and the first beat staying silent. **Every arm was true.** A Tier 1 reviewer then
drove the *real* `on_frame()` and it raised `UnboundLocalError` on the first healthy heartbeat.

**Root cause (mine, and a repeat).** I inserted the `global _last_owned` declaration with a regex
anchored on `_stall_frames` — a substring that appears in the `global` line of **both** `enable()`
and `on_frame()`. `re.search` returns the first, so the declaration landed in the function that never
assigns the name, while the function that does kept treating it as a **local**.
⛔ **And it would not have failed loudly:** `main.py:101-107` wraps the call in `except Exception:
pass`, so the result was **every heartbeat line gone, on every run, forever** — including the
`party_ids` field shipped hours earlier that the next queued measurement depends on. **A telemetry
change that disables telemetry, invisibly.**

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — TEST THE FUNCTION THE PRODUCTION LOOP CALLS, NOT THE HELPERS IT CALLS.** My
five arms exercised `_owned_dex()` and the delta arithmetic *in isolation*; the integration — the
`global` scoping, the heartbeat condition, the write — was never executed. ⇒ **a suite that never
invokes the production entry point cannot detect an integration bug, no matter how many arms it
has.** This is project rule §7 (*instrument the ACTION, not the input to the action*) restated for
tests, and it is the SAME shape as the gate error logged hours earlier the same day: **a green check
on something adjacent to the thing under test.** ⇒ before believing a suite, ask *"which line of
production code does this actually run?"*

**⭐ Second rule, narrower and mechanical: AN EDIT ANCHOR MUST BE UNIQUE — ASSERT THE COUNT.** Every
doc edit in this project asserts `t.count(OLD) == 1`; I used a bare `re.search` for a *code* edit and
it silently took the first of two matches. **Same discipline, both file types.** ⇒ this is the third
"a substring is not a message" failure logged this session, and the first one in a code edit rather
than a log grep — the pattern is not about logs, it is about **anchoring on something that does not
uniquely identify the target.**

**✅ THE DURABLE FIX IS A GATE, NOT A RULE: `tools/story-dev/repro_heartbeat_emits.py`** drives the
real `on_frame()` across two heartbeats and asserts on the real log file. Fault-tested: with the
`global` removed it reports `UnboundLocalError` and **0** heartbeat lines.
‼ Its own first version produced a **FALSE FAIL** on correct code — it passed the frame count as an
argument, but `on_frame` reads it from `_light_state()["frame"]`. The existing rule *"when a probe
FAILS, read the failing line before touching the thing under test"* is what prevented me from
'fixing' code that was already right. **That rule has now paid for itself four times.**

## 2026-09-09 — A new gate's self-tests passed; the real tree failed it on the first run

**Symptom.** I wrote `check_gate_arithmetic` to catch a self-contradicting sentence (*"49 gates
(46 ENFORCING + 2 ADVISORY)"*), gave it five self-tests, and all five passed — including a
deliberate no-false-positive case. Run against the actual documentation it **immediately fired on
correct text**: `gates|entries` was optional in the pattern, so the leading `(\d+)` captured the `0`
from *"must exit 0; the suite is 49 gates …"*.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — RUN A NEW GATE OVER THE REAL CORPUS BEFORE TRUSTING ITS SELF-TESTS.**
Synthetic cases are written from the same mental model as the pattern, so they share its blind spots:
not one of my five had a number earlier in the line, because I was not *thinking* about preceding
numbers. **The corpus contains shapes the author did not imagine — that is the entire reason it is
worth checking.** ⇒ every new gate gets one real-tree run before it is believed, and any false
positive found there becomes a permanent self-test (here, **GA6**).
‼ This is the same shape as the failure logged hours earlier — *five test arms that never called the
function under test*. **Both are "the test exercised what I was already thinking about."**

**‼ AND A RULE I BROKE WHILE FIXING IT.** I edited `audit_doc_consistency.py` by piping Python
through a shell, against this project's explicit rule to *write file-editing Python to a FILE*. The
shell expanded a `\n` inside a nested string, producing an unterminated literal — and because the
write happened before the `ast.parse` check, **it left the gate file broken on disk**.
⇒ **A RULE I CAN RECITE IS NOT A RULE I FOLLOW UNDER MOMENTUM.** I quoted a different rule at myself
one command earlier. The protection is structural, not mental: **the edit goes in a file, and the
file parses before it is written** — order matters, `ast.parse` BEFORE `write_text`, not after.

## 2026-09-09 — The queued next action would have run the wrong fork and produced a false negative

**Symptom (caught before spending it, not after).** Three documents — the handoff banner, the live
queue, and the owning punch-list item — instructed the next session to *"run ONE ORDINARY batch"* to
settle two questions I had just unblocked with new telemetry. Before starting it I checked which fork
the batch runner drives: **`x4_headless.py` sets `BUILD_NAME = "custom"`**, deliberately, so that a
batch measures the fork that holds still. **Both new fields are sandbox-only** — measured:
`custom-pokebot/modules/debug_logger.py` contains `party_ids` **0** times and `_owned_dex` **0** times.

⇒ the instruction as written burns hours of runtime and emits **no `ids=`, no `owned=`, no `[DEX]`**.
⛔ **And the failure would not have looked like a failure.** The natural reading of an empty result is
*"the data does not support the claim"* — a **FALSE NEGATIVE wearing the costume of an answer**, on
the exact figure (*"88.8% born behind"*) that decides where the next month of work goes.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — AN INSTRUCTION TO "RUN X" MUST NAME THE BUILD IT RUNS AGAINST WHENEVER THE
THING BEING MEASURED IS NOT YET PROMOTED.** New instrumentation lives in the sandbox by definition,
and the batch runner defaults to custom by design; those two correct decisions compose into a silent
trap **every single time**, so the flag belongs in the instruction, not in the reader's memory.

**‼ AND THE PART THAT SHOULD WORRY A FUTURE AGENT: THIS PASSED EVERYTHING.** P1-P5 all agreed, three
gates were green, and two Tier 1 reviews had read the surrounding text. **Consistency checks cannot
see a missing flag** — every document said the same true-but-unusable thing. It is the same class as
the handed-off A/B whose named fixture made both arms identical: *perfectly self-consistent and
perfectly vacuous*. ⇒ **the strongest test of a handoff is not "do its halves agree?" but "does
following it literally produce the measurement it promises?"** — which is exactly what Tier 2's
"try to BEGIN the next item" clause is for, and why that clause outranks the pair checks.

## 2026-09-09 — I measured a proxy, then let an unweighted median hide the answer

**Two errors in one measurement, both caught before publication, both worth the entry.**

**(1) THE PROXY.** Asked *"does swap-training split the exp?"*, my first tool counted **how many mon
gained** per swap-training window and found 2 in 11 of 14. That number is real and **cannot answer
the question**: two mon gaining the same amount is equally consistent with *"each banks a full
share"* and *"each banks half"*. ⇒ **the action is the AMOUNT; the count is a proxy for it.** The
honest test was a controlled comparison — same foe species AND level, 1 participant vs 2 — which
used **3,446 ordinary battles** instead of the 14 rare windows.
⭐ **PREVENTION RULE — WHEN A MEASUREMENT IS ABOUT A MAGNITUDE, COUNTING THE EVENTS IS NOT MEASURING
IT.** And note where the evidence came from: **the rare event was not the evidence.** If the
interesting case is rare, look for an ORDINARY case that discriminates the same hypotheses — it will
have hundreds of times the sample.

**(2) THE STATISTIC ATE THE RESULT.** The corrected tool then printed **0.838 — INCONCLUSIVE**, while
its own table showed the largest-sample groups at 0.50-0.54. *(⚠ NOT 'every' large-sample group — a
Tier 1 reviewer was right to refuse that word: `Poochyena L6` 0.83 and `Nincada L6` 0.81 both carry
n2=13. Real heterogeneity, plausibly the decomp's `calculatedExp / 2 / viaExpShare` second regime.)*
Cause: it took an **unweighted median across 87 foe-groups**, so a group with n2=7 outvoted one with n2=29, and a stratum of 30 tiny
noisy groups (ratio 1.18, none surviving n2>=10) dragged the headline up.
⭐⭐ **PREVENTION RULE — AN UNWEIGHTED MEDIAN OVER GROUPS SUMMARISES THE GROUPS, NOT THE
OBSERVATIONS.** Stratify and show the CONVERGENCE (0.838 → 0.624 → 0.586 → 0.520 as min n2 rises);
a single number that can be dominated by the noisiest cells is not a summary, it is a coin flip with
a decimal point. ⇒ **when a headline contradicts the table above it, the headline is the bug.**
‼ This is the same family as the sampling error logged an hour earlier (`logs[:400]` of a sorted
list) — **three times in one day the DATA was fine and the way I reduced it was not.**

## 2026-09-09 — A regex that dropped every status-afflicted battler: 13.5% of rows, and not at random

**Symptom.** A Tier 1 reviewer refused a published figure — I wrote *"30 of 31 rotations were turn>0
and hurt"*; a direct `grep` found **32** rotations (31 hurt + 1 full-HP). One row off, in a 32-row
sample.

**Root cause, and it was far larger than the symptom.** My `[TURN]` pattern required
`(\d+)/(\d+)\s*->`, but a battler carrying a status logs `3/23 [Infatuated] -> RotateLead`. Across
the batch that shape silently discards **7,620 of 56,339 turn lines — 13.5%**: 2,490 Paralysis,
2,014 Confused, 849 Sleep, 600 Poison, 560 Sleep/Confused, 283 Infatuated...
⛔ **The dropped rows are NOT random. They are the battles going badly — precisely where a rotation
is likeliest** — so every rate computed from that pattern was biased in the direction that mattered.

**‼ THE PATTERN LIVED IN A FILE WHOSE OWN DOCSTRING WARNS ABOUT THIS.**
`probe_swaptrain_envelope.py` says *"A PARSER THAT LOSES ROWS INFLATES EVERY RATE AND ANNOUNCES
NOTHING"* — written after fixing a **different** over-tightening in the **same** pattern. **One hole
was found and fixed; the other sat beside it untouched.**

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN YOU CORRECT A PARSER, RE-MEASURE ITS DENOMINATOR AGAINST THE RAW LINE
COUNT, NOT AGAINST THE PREVIOUS PARSE.** `48,719 parsed of 56,339 raw` was computable at any moment
by anyone who compared the two numbers; nobody did, because a parse that returns tens of thousands of
rows looks healthy **on its own**. ⇒ a parser's health is a RATIO to the unfiltered corpus, and it
belongs in the tool's own output.

**⭐ AND THE SECOND LESSON — IMPACT IS PER-TOOL, SO MEASURE IT PER TOOL.** The same 13.5% hole:
* **material** for the divisor tool (uses all battles): n2>=10 went 0.586 → **0.504**, i.e. the bug
  had been *hiding* the true 0.5;
* **negligible** for the envelope tool: 24,244 → 25,914 decisions, gap +2 rate 29.9% → **30.1%**, and
  every published conclusion survived — because it already filtered to turn-0 **full-HP**, where a
  status is rare.
⇒ **"a shared parser was wrong" does not imply "every result from it was wrong".** Re-run each
consumer and report the delta; announcing a blanket invalidation would have been as inaccurate as
the bug, and would have thrown away sound measurements.

## 2026-09-09 — The number replicated and the sentence built on it was false

**Symptom.** I set out to check a figure — *"88.8% of laggards were already >6 behind when first
seen"* — because it was deciding where effort went. It replicated: I measured **84.1%**, and 88.8%
sits inside the measurement's own CI. Had I stopped there I would have written *"claim confirmed"*
and moved on. **The sentence the number supported — "so there is no early small-gap window to
maintain" — is false: 39.7% of that very population HAD a window**, median 163 heartbeats.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A STATISTIC AND THE INFERENCE DRAWN FROM IT ARE TWO CLAIMS, AND VERIFYING
THE FIRST SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE SECOND.** "Most arrive past the threshold" and "there was never a
window" are compatible-sounding and independently checkable, and only the second one routed the
decision. ⇒ **when a claim is cited to justify an action, test the SENTENCE THAT JUSTIFIES THE
ACTION, not the number in front of it.** The number is usually the easy half and rarely the load-
bearing one.

**⭐ WHAT MADE THIS WORK: refuters, not more measurers.** Five angles each got a separate agent whose
only job was to refute it; **three of five headlines were refuted by their own refuter** while their
arithmetic survived intact. That asymmetry is the finding — *the measurements were right and the
sentences around them overreached*, which is exactly the failure a second measurer would have
reproduced rather than caught.

**⭐⭐ AND A UNIT-CHOICE TRAP WORTH ITS OWN LINE.** One angle reported *"roughly half the debt is
accrued AFTER arrival (44.8%)"*. Its refuter re-ran the identical windows in different units:
**44.8% in levels, 71.9% in absolute exp, 4.3% in relative exp.** Same mons, same windows, three
answers spanning the entire range. ⇒ **when a quantity can be measured in more than one unit, the
unit IS the finding** — report it in every unit that a reader might assume, or the number means
nothing. Levels are not linear in experience, and any "how much of the gap" claim measured in levels
is a statement about the level curve as much as about the bot.

**‼ A defect in my own week-old work, found the same way:** `party_ids` treats PID as identity, and
**PID is not unique** — Shedinja is created as a copy of Nincada and inherits its personality value
(1,360 heartbeats measured). A field I shipped this morning promised an identity it does not have.
⇒ **before shipping an identity key, ask what the GAME does that can duplicate it** — evolution,
cloning, trades — rather than assuming a value called "personality" is one.

## 2026-09-09 (late) — Three failures in one day, one cause: I read the verdict and not the output

**Refining a rule I wrote earlier today, because I diagnosed it wrongly.** I logged *"a green gate is
evidence only about the files it READS — before citing a gate, read its SCOPE/BUDGETS."* True, but it
blames the tools, and the tools were innocent: **both gates I mis-cited ALREADY PRINT their scope.**
`repro_no_silent_except.py` prints a per-root budget table; `repro_undefined_names.py` prints
*"‼ Note the deliberate scope: ..."*. The information was on screen. I quoted the exit code.

**The same shape happened three times today:**

| what I quoted | what the output actually said |
|---|---|
| two gates' PASS, as validating a new handler | their scope table — the file was not in it |
| a background task's "exit code 0" | the suite's own `exit=1` (0 was the shell WRAPPER's) |
| my own tool's headline "INCONCLUSIVE" | its table, showing 0.50 in every large-sample group |

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A VERDICT IS A SUMMARY, AND THE SUMMARY IS NOT THE EVIDENCE. READ THE OUTPUT
THAT QUALIFIES IT BEFORE QUOTING IT.** Specifically: an exit code says a process ended, not what it
checked; a PASS says the checks that RAN passed; a headline says what its author's statistic
concluded, not what the table shows. ⇒ **when you cite a tool, cite a LINE OF ITS OUTPUT, not its
status** — and if the line you would quote does not exist, you have not actually verified anything.
‼ Corollary earned the same day: **when a tool prints two verdicts, say out loud which one your claim
rests on.** In the wrapper case both were visible in the same scrollback and I picked the wrong one
twice before noticing.

**⭐ AND WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL RULE: it is cheap to follow and it caught real bugs
every time it was applied.** Reading the failing line (rather than assuming the subject was broken)
is what prevented me from "fixing" correct code twice today — once when a probe reported a false
FAIL because it passed the frame count as an argument, and once when a gate's own table refuted its
headline.

## 2026-09-09 — I shipped a units bug in the same commit where I wrote "the unit IS the finding"

**Symptom.** My tool printed *"median time spent inside the window: 163 heartbeats (~2.7 min)"*. One
heartbeat is `_HEARTBEAT_EVERY = 3600` frames, and at 60fps that is **one minute** — so 163
heartbeats is **163 minutes ≈ 2.7 HOURS**. I had divided by 60 (minutes → hours) and labelled the
result "min". Every digit was correct; only the word was wrong.

**⛔ AND IT INVERTED THE ARGUMENT.** The finding is that laggards had an unused window. *"2.7
minutes"* reads as a window too brief to exploit — evidence AGAINST my own conclusion. *"2.7 hours"*
is an enormous, obviously-actionable window. **A units bug can flip what a result means while
leaving the arithmetic untouched**, which is why it survives every check that looks at numbers.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN A TOOL CONVERTS A UNIT, PRINT BOTH THE RAW COUNT AND THE CONVERSION, AND
NAME THE CONVERSION FACTOR IN THE LINE ABOVE IT.** `163 heartbeats = 163 min (~2.7 hours)` is
self-checking; `~2.7 min` is not, because nothing in it can be compared against anything. ⇒ a lone
converted number is unverifiable by construction — the reader cannot see the factor you used.

**‼ THE PART WORTH SITTING WITH: I WROTE THE RULE AND BROKE IT IN THE SAME COMMIT.** That commit's own
mistakes entry says *"when a quantity can be measured in more than one unit, the unit IS the
finding"* — a lesson from a refuter showing that "half the debt" was 44.8% in levels, 71.9% in
absolute exp and 4.3% in relative exp. **Writing a rule is not installing it.** The rule that
actually caught this was not prose at all: it was an independent reviewer with a mandate to attack,
and the fix that persists is the tool printing its own conversion factor.

**⭐ SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME REVIEW, AND IT IS A REAL METHOD RULE: A GAP CLOSES FROM EITHER END.**
I counted 15 mons that "recovered into the training window". Decomposed: **11 levelled up into it**
(actionable — training reached them) and **4 had the party MAX FALL** (the leader was deposited or
swapped; level never drops on a faint), which opens a window the bot did nothing to earn. ⇒ the
headline 39.7% stands as "had a window", but the number a FIX can act on is **33.3%**. **When a
difference narrows, always ask WHICH side moved** — only one of them is usually something you can
cause.

## 2026-09-09 — My measurement used a window one level wider than the code it was measuring

**Symptom.** I published "33.3% of laggards were TRAINING-REACHABLE" hours after correcting, in the
same commit, the very predicate it depends on. My tool called a mon inside the window at `gap <= 6`;
the code is `level >= target - 6` with `target = team_max + 1`, i.e. **`gap <= 5`**. Re-measured:
**20.6%, not 33.3%** — and the "arrived already inside" cohort collapsed from 10 to 1, because nine
of those ten arrived at *exactly* gap 6, the single value the predicate excludes.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN YOU CORRECT A PREDICATE, RE-DERIVE EVERY NUMBER THAT WAS MEASURED WITH
THE OLD ONE, IN THE SAME COMMIT.** I did the hard half (reading the source, finding that
`TRAIN_CATCHUP_GAP` keys on `target` and not the team max) and then reported a statistic built on the
version I had just disproved. ⇒ **a correction is not complete until its consequences are propagated
into the measurements, not merely into the prose.** The tell: my own tool's constant was named
`TRAIN_CATCHUP_GAP` and used as a gap threshold — the name matched the code while the *semantics*
did not, which is exactly why it read as correct.

**⭐ AND THE ERROR WAS PRODUCTIVE, WHICH IS WORTH NOTING HONESTLY.** Chasing the off-by-one produced
the arrival distribution: **48 mons arrive at gap 0, only 12 across gaps 1-5, then 23/36/26 at gaps
6/7/8.** 46% of arrivals land in a three-level band immediately OUTSIDE a window that ends at 5.
⇒ a boundary discrepancy of one level is worth chasing precisely because thresholds sit where the
mass is, and an off-by-one at a threshold is never a rounding detail — **it is the difference between
capturing the mode and missing it entirely.**

## 2026-09-09 — A strong-looking lead, killed by the angle I told to disbelieve it

**Symptom.** I found what looked like a real defect: 46% of party arrivals cluster at gaps 6-8, the
training window ends at gap 5, so mons land systematically just outside the door. Clean histogram,
obvious mechanism, an actionable one-constant fix. **All of it was wrong**, and the parts that were
right were already known.

**⭐⭐ WHAT SAVED IT: I built the disconfirming angle INTO the investigation rather than hoping to
notice later.** One of the five agents was told *"you are the designated skeptic; default to 'the
premise is an artifact' and make the evidence force you off it"*, and it is the one that landed —
along with a counterfactual angle whose only job was to PRICE the fix rather than argue for it. ⇒
**when you have a hypothesis you like, commission its refutation in the same breath as its
investigation.** Adding a skeptic afterwards costs a build; adding one upfront costs one agent.

**⭐ THE SPECIFIC ERROR WORTH REMEMBERING: I counted "party arrivals" and called them "catches".**
95 of my 184 were starters, tutorial handouts, gift mons, PC withdrawals — and **27 were an
opponent's allies merged into the party by a multi-battle**, which I had not imagined as a way for a
Pokémon to appear. The gap-0 spike that made the distribution look bimodal was entirely
non-catches. ⇒ **when a population is defined by an EVENT, anchor on the event's own log line, never
on the state change it usually causes.** "The party grew" has at least six causes here; "a Caught
line fired" has one.

**⛔⛔ AND THE RULE I ALREADY HAD AND STILL DID NOT FOLLOW: GREP `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` FIRST.** *(⚠ and when I finally did, I OVERCLAIMED it: the entry's subject is `mon.level + 3`, a different constant — the reasoning transfers, the ruling does not. A reviewer had flagged that caveat and I dropped it while summarising, which is the same 'degraded in transit' failure I had criticised an agent for hours earlier.)* A dated
entry (`:267-269`, five weeks old) rejects exactly this class of fix — *"any level-denominated
threshold is wrong… it cannot see the XP rate; tuning it just moves which map it is wrong on"*. My
own standing rule says to search that file before escalating or proposing, precisely because it
exists so a question is never answered twice. An agent found it, not me.
⇒ the rule needs a **trigger**, not more emphasis: **before investigating any CONSTANT, grep the
decisions log for the constant's name AND for its class ("threshold", "window", "level").** The cost
of not doing it here was one workflow; the value recovered was that a reasoned ruling now has a
measurement behind it, which is not nothing — but it was not the plan.

⛔ **An agent had already flagged that caveat and I dropped it while summarising** — the identical
"degraded in transit" failure I had criticised an agent for hours earlier. ⇒ **when a source you are
compressing carries a caveat about its own scope, the caveat travels with the claim or the claim does
not travel.**

## 2026-09-10 — Twice in two days the argument that killed my design was already in the repo

**Symptom.** I diagnosed the §Ch23 refusal (HM carriers, Marill 11/23 events), proposed the obvious
narrow fix (add Marill to `BENCH_SPECIES`), and ran the prior-art rule I had written the day before.
**I still missed the argument that kills it** — `07-CHANGELOG.md` F6: *"'bench' means only 'do not
train' — the mon is still FIELDED"*. An agent found it. That is the SECOND consecutive design killed
by something already written down here.

**⛔ AND THE RULE WAS NOT THE PROBLEM — MY SEARCH WAS.** I grepped `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` for
`BENCH_SPECIES` and for "bench by role", and got one hit each. The killing argument lived in a
**different file** under **different words**. ⇒ I searched for the SYMBOL I intended to CHANGE, and
the objection was phrased in terms of the MECHANISM I intended to RELY ON.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION — MADE A TOOL, NOT A RULE, BECAUSE THE RULE HAD ALREADY FAILED ONCE:**
`tools/story-dev/precheck_prior_art.py` sweeps all five history/status files for any number of terms
and flags hits sitting within a few lines of a verdict word. **Fault-tested against the real miss**:
`precheck_prior_art.py "still FIELDED" "do not train"` → `07-CHANGELOG.md:24731 ⛔ VERDICT WORD NEARBY`.
‼ The habit it encodes: **list what your fix RELIES ON, not only what it CHANGES, and search both.**
A bench fix relies on "benched mons stay out of battles" — that sentence is where its refutation
lives, and no `BENCH_SPECIES` grep will ever reach it.

**⭐ SECOND LESSON, FROM THE SAME ROUND — AN ARGMAX CANNOT BE COUNTED BY NAME.** I counted which
species the refusal names (Marill 48%) and inferred what removing it would fix. But the refusal takes
`max(estimates)`: it names exactly ONE mon, so the name-count says nothing about what removal clears.
Measured properly it clears **6-10 of 23**, not 48%, and the residual is a mon that can never be
benched. ⇒ **when a check reports an ARGMAX, the population it names is not the population it
blocks** — re-price the whole set with the candidate applied, per event.

**⭐ THIRD, SMALLER: MY 414 WAS RIGHT AND STILL MISLEADING.** An agent accused the figure of being
irreproducible; its own refuter defended it (`grep -ro "alone needs" */*/stdout.txt | wc -l` → 414,
exactly as stated, correctly scoped to "all of x4-runs"). But each refusal event renders **18 times**
in stdout and 15 in debug-logs ⇒ the decision unit is **23 events**. **A correct count of the wrong
unit is still the wrong number for the decision** — state the unit beside every count.

## 2026-09-10 — New evidence appeared to overturn a settled ruling; measured, it confirmed it

**Symptom (a good outcome, recorded so the METHOD is repeatable).** I measured that `Marill` causes
11 of 23 §Ch23 refusals, and a 2026-08-13 user-delegated ruling had kept the Route 117 hunting
ground while calling its L13 learner *"quality, not capability"*. That looked like a settled decision
resting on a premise I had just refuted — the strongest legitimate ground for re-opening one.

**⭐⭐ WHAT I DID INSTEAD OF RE-OPENING IT: PRICED THE PREMISE FIRST.** The ruling's claim is
falsifiable in one calculation — does a higher-level carrier clear the gate? Using the bot's own
estimator with constants read from source: **L13 → 406,972 frames, L25 → 352,518, L27 → 336,755,
against a 250,000 ceiling. All three refuse.** The premise holds; the ruling stands; my
re-prioritisation was wrong before I proposed it.
⇒ **PREVENTION RULE — WHEN NEW EVIDENCE SEEMS TO OVERTURN A SETTLED DECISION, TEST THE DECISION'S
OWN STATED PREMISE BEFORE RE-OPENING IT.** A ruling usually names the belief it rests on; that belief
is a claim, and claims are cheaper to check than decisions are to re-litigate. ‼ And write the
disconfirming branch INTO the tool — mine printed *"the ruling's premise stands"* on its own, which
is far harder to argue with than a conclusion I reasoned to afterwards.

**⭐ THE VALIDATION STEP EARNED MORE THAN THE MEASUREMENT.** I checked the growth curve against real
logged values rather than trusting the formula, and found **521 of 521 Marill sightings at
`L13:exp1757`** — an exact curve match AND the discovery that the carrier **never gains any exp at
all**. ⇒ **validate a model against real data even when you are confident, because the validation
sees things the model was not asked about.** The calculation answered "would a better ground help?";
the validation answered "what IS this mon?", which is the more useful question.

**‼ AND THE PRIOR-ART TOOL PAID FOR ITSELF ON ITS FIRST REAL USE.** `precheck_prior_art.py "Marill"
"carrier" "Route 104"` surfaced **7 decisions-log hits** — including the binding ruling — that no
grep for the symbol I intended to change (`BENCH_SPECIES`) would ever have reached. It also surfaced
`#24-divegroundroute120`, a filed, spec'd, unbuilt item that was exactly the idea I was forming.
⇒ **the tool did not just prevent a mistake; it found the prior work I was about to duplicate.**

## 2026-09-10 — I made a test MANDATORY and it was vacuous for the thing it was testing

**Symptom.** Having learned that the 2026-09-08 design died because nobody ran it on the known-good
fixture, I made that test process-mandatory in my next investigation — any refuter that skipped it
returned REFUTED. **For the predicate under test it was vacuous.** Every member of that fixture sits
far above its capture level, so *"has never gained exp since capture"* benches nobody there and
"passes" while discriminating nothing.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A MANDATORY CHECK MUST BE ONE THE CANDIDATE COULD FAIL. BEFORE REQUIRING A
TEST, ASK WHAT RESULT WOULD COUNT AS FAILING IT.** I imported a check that had real discriminating
power against a LEVEL-GAP predicate (which does bench L40/L42 mons) and applied it to an
EXP-SINCE-CAPTURE predicate, where it cannot fire. ⇒ **a test inherits its power from the candidate,
not from its history** — "this killed the last design" is not a reason to expect it to test the next
one. The generalisation of the project's own vacuous-A/B rule, now demonstrated on a check I wrote
myself, one day after writing the rule.

**⭐ SECOND — AND THIS ONE IS A SCOPE ERROR I HAVE NOW LOGGED THREE TIMES IN TWO DAYS.** I published
*"all 521 Marill sightings read L13:exp1757 — the carrier NEVER gains a point"*. It was true of the
**one batch that carries per-mon exp**, and false of the corpus: across all 33 Marill-carrying logs
there are **1,492 readings above L13**. I had the corpus available and measured the sample.
⇒ **when a finding says NEVER, widen the corpus before writing the word.** "Never" is the single
most scope-sensitive claim available, and the cost of checking it was one grep.

**⭐ THIRD — CENSORING MASQUERADING AS A PROPERTY.** "The carrier never gains exp" was also an
artifact of the observation window: the slowest observed gainer needed **157 minutes**, and **25 of
28 non-gainers were watched for less time than that**. ⇒ **before calling an absence a property, ask
how long you would have had to watch to see it** — a run that ends early makes every slow process
look like no process.

**⭐ WHAT WENT RIGHT, AND IS WORTH REPEATING: THE KILL WAS A PROOF, NOT A STATISTIC.** Four mons
caught byte-identical (`Abra L7:exp236`), three trained to Kadabra L17-L20, one inert. **A single
counter-example quartet settled a question that no amount of aggregate measurement would have** —
because it demonstrates non-separability directly rather than estimating it. ⇒ when assessing a
predicate, look first for two items it must treat identically and that the world treats differently.

## 2026-09-10 — I wrote "the tree is clean and pushed" inside an uncommitted edit

**Symptom.** The session-end Tier 2 cold-start audit ran `git status`, found
` M "PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/04-HANDOFF.md"`, and pointed out that the uncommitted block's own text read
*"Nothing is parked mid-task; the tree is clean and pushed."* **The sentence was false at the moment
it was read, because the sentence WAS the uncommitted change.**

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A CLAIM ABOUT THE WORKING TREE CANNOT LIVE UN-ANCHORED IN THE WORKING TREE.**
Any "clean / pushed / nothing parked" statement must either name the COMMIT it is true as of, or
tell the reader to check `git status` instead of believing it. ⇒ the handoff now says *"state is
true as of the commit carrying this line — verify with `git status`, never from this sentence."*
‼ The general form: **a document asserting a fact about its own storage is self-refuting while it is
unsaved.** The same shape would bite any "all gates green" line written before the gates are re-run.

**⭐ SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME AUDIT — A CONVENTION THAT GUARDS ONE MARKER SHAPE DOES NOT GUARD THE
OTHERS.** The handoff has a rule that *"more than one `➡➡➡` here is a DEFECT"*, and it holds — there
is exactly one. But a SECOND imperative list, written with a single `➡`, still commanded
`#24-ch23training`, work that is now diagnosed and whose upstream target is declared dead-ended six
lines above it. The convention never covered it because it was written about one glyph.
⇒ **when you invent a marker convention, enumerate every marker shape already in the file** — the
stale instruction will use the shape your rule forgot. Fixed by marking that list SUPERSEDED rather
than deleting it (its citations are still good).

## 2026-09-10 — I nearly archived a CLOSED item that was the only tracker of an OPEN task

**Symptom (caught before it shipped, not after).** `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` sat at exactly its 4,200-line
R3 cap, so the handoff’s “ARCHIVE FIRST, WRITE SECOND” instruction applied. I selected archive
candidates by a property that sounded sufficient: **`###` sections containing zero `- [ ]` / `- [~]`
boxes.** `#24-e4moveset` qualified — header says CLOSED, every checkbox ticked, work genuinely done.

**The assumption that proved wrong.** *“An item with no open checkboxes owns no open facts.”* Its
final paragraph, headed “**WHAT REMAINS (not this item)**”, named the un-fetched **Dragon Claw
(TM02) for Sceptile**. A `grep -n “Dragon Claw|TM02”` across `03`/`04`/`05` returned **exactly one
hit — that line.** The tree had no other record of it. Archiving on the checkbox rule would have
retired the sole tracker of a live §0 pickup that the §Ch24 Drake fight is argued to need.

**Root cause.** A checkbox is a claim about the ITEM’S OWN work. Prose inside the block can be a
claim about SOMEONE ELSE’S — and the phrase that marks it (“not this item”) is precisely the phrase
that makes it invisible to any per-item status scan. The scan and the hazard are orthogonal.

**The fix that worked.** Grep the block for its own nouns BEFORE retiring it, and count hits
**outside** the block. Zero outside hits = the block is the sole owner = hoist that sentence into
the stub. Done here: the residual now lives in `03`, the rest is verbatim in `28`.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *“Closed” describes the work, not every sentence in the block —
before archiving an item, grep its body’s nouns tree-wide and hoist anything it solely owns.*

‼ **Generalises past archiving.** This is the same shape as P5 (a fact living in three places, two
updated): **a per-item check protects exactly what it enumerates.** A checkbox scan enumerates
checkboxes. It was never going to see a prose to-do, and its PASS reads as safety.

## 2026-09-10 — A guard that reads a FLAG cannot see a resource being spent BEFORE the flag is set

**Symptom (caught in code review, before any drive).** `#24-dexhunt`'s fence was specified as
*"catch only when no hunt is armed"* — `not counter_hunt.is_armed()`. It reads as airtight: the hunt
owns a shared resource, so gate on "is the hunt running?".

**The assumption that proved wrong.** *"A subsystem is protected while its own ARMED flag is set."*
`counter_hunt.hunt()` verifies its Poke Balls at `counter_hunt.py:471`, TRAVELS at `:488`
(`_navigate_riding_out(..., tries=24)`, which that function's own comment calls *"the LONGEST journey
the bot ever makes ... 8 map-hops away across several warp chains"*), and only calls `arm()` at `:510`.
=> **The window in which the hunt is most vulnerable is exactly the window in which its flag is
FALSE.** The fence would have been free to spend the balls the hunt had already counted, all the way
down to its own floor, during the trek. The hunt does not re-check on arrival: it arms, spins the
full `HUNT_SPIN_BUDGET_FRAMES` (120,000) and reports *"found nothing"* while standing on the answer —
the exact failure that block's own comment says the feature suffered once already.

**Root cause.** A boolean flag records that a subsystem is IN ITS CRITICAL SECTION. It says nothing
about that subsystem having ALREADY COMMITTED to a resource. Verification and arming were separated
by the single longest journey in the program, and nothing in between held a claim on the balls.

**The fix that worked.** Make the guard a LEVEL, not a flag: `DEX_CATCH_BALL_RESERVE = 10`, kept
deliberately separate from `resource_blocker()`'s floor of 1 (correct for a MANDATORY catch, wrong
for a discretionary one). A reserve is true across the whole journey; a flag is not.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *When a guard protects a shared resource, gate on the RESOURCE
LEVEL, not on a flag saying someone is using it — find where the flag is SET relative to where the
resource is CLAIMED, and ask what runs in between.*

‼ **The shape generalises past balls.** Before trusting any `is_X_active()` guard, locate the SET
site and the COMMIT site. Here they were ~40 lines and one cross-Hoenn walk apart.

⛔ **AND A SECOND LESSON FROM THE SAME ROUND: my first write-up of the collision was WRONG, and a
refuter caught it.** I wrote that an off-type dex catch during an armed hunt would be REGISTERED as
the counter. It would not — the hunt's verdict is TYPE-AWARE (`party_counter_slot` /
`box_counter_pid`, `counter_hunt.py:546`/`:559`). The harm is real but quieter: the species-BLIND box
path in `catch_confirmed` (`:363-365`) ENDS THE SPIN EARLY, and the type-aware verdict then finds
nothing — losing a 120,000-frame hunt and a ball.
=> **The guard was right and my REASON for it was wrong.** That would have shipped a correct fence
carrying a comment that misleads the next reader into deleting it. A refuter is the only reviewer
that catches a true conclusion resting on a false mechanism, because a second measurer reproduces
the conclusion and stops.

## 2026-09-10 — I refactored a predicate into a pure function and silently changed the case I had just promised not to touch

**Symptom (caught by MY OWN A/B, before commit — but only because I ran one).** Extracting
`_should_catch`'s logic into the pure `decide_dex_catch` collapsed three different party figures into
one parameter, `party_slots_used`. The pre-gym-1 branch then tested that RAW count against
`_catch_team_target`. The old code tested an EGG-FILTERED count.
=> **3 battlers + 1 egg** read as a full team of 4 and REFUSED a catch the old code ALLOWED.

**Why it survived review — mine and the design's.** The two counts are *identical* unless an egg is in
the party. Every case I had written, every case a reviewer would think to write, and all 18 cases of
the new gate used egg-free parties. The refactor looked like a pure move of existing logic, and it
read like one. **The divergence had exactly one witness and I had not invited it.**

**Root cause.** One name, `party_slots_used`, was serving three questions that an egg answers
differently:
  * *"will the game box this catch?"* — eggs COUNT (the game counts an occupied slot);
  * *"how big is the TEAM?"* — eggs DO NOT (a target for things that can fight);
  * *"do we already own this species?"* — eggs DO NOT.
A refactor that unifies parameters is exactly where such a distinction dies, because the collapsing
is the point of the refactor.

**The fix that worked.** Two parameters, `party_slots_used` (raw) and `battler_count` (egg-filtered),
each documented with the question it answers — plus, crucially, a PROOF rather than a re-read:

    5,760 pre-gym-1 input combinations compared against the OLD logic transcribed from git
    history (wild/shiny/dex-flag x balls x battlers x EGGS x species x owned x party) => 0 divergences.

Cases C19/C20 in `probe_dex_catch_fence.py` are that A/B kept as a permanent regression test, and
C15 is deliberately the SAME party shape read by the other convention.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *When a refactor unifies two parameters into one, find the input
on which they DISAGREE and make it a test case — if you cannot name one, they were not two
parameters.*

‼ **The wider rule this cost me:** "behaviour is unchanged" is a CLAIM, and this project's currency
for a claim is an arm. I wrote "the ordinary case must stay byte-identical" in the code comments
BEFORE I had run anything that could tell. A comment asserting equivalence is worth nothing next to
a grid that demonstrates it — and the grid took under a minute.

## 2026-09-10 — The tool that enforces "check prior art" had a blind spot, and reported "none" over an existing answer

**Symptom.** Before proposing a §Ch24 entry marker I ran the project's own
`tools/story-dev/precheck_prior_art.py` — the tool CLAUDE.md requires before any new design — on
`SYS_GAME_CLEAR`, "progress marker", `ResetEliteFour` and "re-entered". It reported essentially
nothing, so I commissioned a four-agent decomp round to work the design out from scratch.
An adversarial refuter then found the identical recommendation ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, in two places:
`ai-research-notes/2026-09-07-ch24-elite-four-BUILD-SPEC.md:70` and
`2026-09-08-ch24-league-RECON.md:39`.

**Root cause, verified in one line.** `precheck_prior_art.py:36` —
`FILES = ("05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md", "06-DECISIONS-LOG.md", "07-CHANGELOG.md", "08-MISTAKES.md",
"03-PUNCH-LIST.md")`. Five files. **`ai-research-notes/` held 129 more, and the tool never opened
one of them.** It did not disagree with those notes; it could not see them.

**Why it went unnoticed for so long.** The tool answers CONFIDENTLY either way. "0 hits" reads as
*"nobody has been here"*, never as *"I did not look there"* — coverage was invisible in the output,
so there was nothing to be suspicious of.

⭐ **THE IRONY IS THE LESSON.** This tool's own header records that it exists because a previous
search was TOO NARROW: *"the rule was not wrong, my SEARCH was too narrow."* It then shipped with a
too-narrow search of its own.
⇒ **A TOOL THAT ENFORCES A RULE IS NOT EXEMPT FROM THAT RULE.**

**The fix that worked, PROVEN not asserted.** The tool now scans the five ruling files first, then
every `ai-research-notes/*.md`, and prints its COVERAGE in the footer so "0 hits" can never again be
read without knowing what was searched. A/B on a phrase that exists only in a note
("no A-press trigger"): OLD scope = **0 hits across all five files**; NEW = found, and flagged as
sitting near a verdict word.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *A search tool must print WHAT IT SEARCHED beside what it found —
"0 hits" without coverage is indistinguishable from "I did not look".*

‼ **And a second-order rule, because this cost a four-agent round:** research notes are where a
design gets WORKED OUT before it is ruled on, so they are the likeliest place to hold the argument
that kills a proposal. They remain NOTES, never truth — but a note you have not read cannot be
weighed at all.

## 2026-09-10 — An agent's conclusion was right, its mechanism was wrong, and I had already copied the mechanism into the docs

**Symptom.** An adversarial refuter reported that §Ch23's leg 4 fires an ocean crossing on re-entry,
*"because `at_ever_grande_top()` is False at the League door"*. The CONCLUSION is correct and it is a
real, serious bug. The **because** is false.

**What was actually true.** `EG_LANDING = (18, 55)`, so the predicate is `y <= 55`. The League door
apron is `(18, 6)`. **6 <= 55, so it already returned True there** — leg 4 skipped correctly at the
door, and always had. The real hole is ONE MAP FURTHER IN: each League room is its own map
(`map_data.py:1037-1051`), so `_on_map(EVER_GRANDE_CITY)` is False *inside the building*, and the
League is not in `VICTORY_ROAD_MAPS` either ⇒ both guards read False.

**The cost, and it had already been incurred.** I did not merely receive the wrong mechanism — I
**wrote it into `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` in the preceding commit**, verbatim, inside a correction block
whose whole purpose was fixing other people's wrong claims. A fix aimed at "the League door" would
have changed a case that was never broken, shipped a green probe over it, and left the real defect
live — the worst of the three possible outcomes, because it looks finished.

**Root cause.** A conclusion and its mechanism are SEPARATE claims with separate evidence. Agreement
on the conclusion (leg 4 fires — true) carries no information about the mechanism (which guard, on
which map, for which reason). I verified the conclusion, found it correct, and let that stand in for
verifying the *reason* — the cheapest possible substitution, and invisible because the headline
checked out.

**The fix that worked.** Read the constant. One `grep` for `EG_LANDING` settled it in seconds, and it
inverted the diagnosis. Then the fix went in the PREDICATE (both call sites mirror by design), and
the probe pins BOTH facts: C1/C2 are the real defect, **C3 is the door apron that was never broken**.
The `=nofix` arm proves both halves at once — C1+C2 red, C3-C7 GREEN.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *A conclusion and its mechanism are two claims — verifying the
conclusion does not verify the "because", and the "because" is what you build against.*

‼ **The tell to watch for:** when a report says "X fails **because** Y", the cheapest check is almost
always to read Y's actual value, not to re-test X. Here that was one grep against one constant.

## 2026-09-10 — P5 fired THREE times in one session; the fix was a skill I already had and was not running

**The pattern, all three the same shape.** A fact lived in N places, I corrected the ones I could
NAME, and the pair check then returned PASS over the one I could not:
1. `18 cases` / `:1612` — fixed in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` + `04-HANDOFF.md`, **missed `07-CHANGELOG.md`**.
2. the leg-4 mechanism — fixed in `03` + appended to `07`/`08`, **missed `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`**,
   which is the file `03` explicitly tells the reader to open first.
3. (earlier) a closed punch-list item that solely owned an open fact.

**Why my own greps kept missing it.** I grepped for what I had CHANGED — the numbers, the symbol
names. The survivor each time was the same claim in DIFFERENT WORDS, or the same words 3,000 lines
away under a pointer. ⛔ **A literal grep proves the absence of a SPELLING, not of a CLAIM.**

**The fix, and it is not another prose rule.** This repo already ships a `staleness-sweep` skill
built for exactly this — proximity search over topic-words × staleness-cues across EVERY
`PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/*.md`, judged by hand. I had not been invoking it.
✅ **RUN IT ON OCCURRENCE 3 AND IT WORKED FIRST TIME:** it surfaced the `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`
survivor (plus 6 legitimate hits I dismissed by hand — my own refuting quotes, and a DIFFERENT
chapter's "leg 4"). A hand-grep for my changed numbers would never have reached it.

⭐ **STANDING RULE, ADOPTED:** *after correcting a CLAIM (not just a number), run `staleness-sweep`
before the commit — and judge every hit by hand, because roughly half are legitimate.*

‼ **And the append-only wrinkle this exposed.** The survivor sat in `06`, which is append-only. The
resolution: **mark in place, rewrite nothing.** Not one word of the original entry changed; a
forward-pointing marker was added beneath it. Append-only protects the RECORD — it does not licence
a file to silently mislead the reader who lands on the wrong claim, especially when another file
points at that exact entry.

## 2026-09-10 — I copied HALF a pattern, and the half I dropped was the half that does the work

**Symptom (caught by a Tier 1 review, before any drive).** Wiring loss-adaptation to two late bosses,
I called `self._prepare_for_fight(cfg)` and stopped. Every other boss wired through that function
since the design matured uses a THREE-line shape:

    yield from self._prepare_for_fight(cfg)
    yield from _lead_best_matchup([...ace_types...], hunted_pids=self._hunted_counter_pids)
    yield from heal_in_pokemon_center(cfg["heal"])

**Why dropping lines 2-3 is worse than shipping nothing.** `_lead_best_matchup` is the SOLE consumer
of `_hunted_counter_pids` — the only thing that FIELDS a hunted counter by moving it to slot 0. So
the counter ladder could spend its one-per-run hunt, cross Hoenn, catch and train a real answer…
and never send it in. Then on the NEXT loss `_boss_plan_is_hopeless`'s party-wide type scan sees that
BENCHED counter as a "credible answer", returns not-hopeless, and **suppresses further escalation and
the honest stop** — while the unchanged lead keeps losing the same way.
⇒ the hunt's entire payoff discarded AND the safety valve disabled: the "guard that now fires on the
healthy path" shape. The party scan looks healthy; the battle is not.

**The assumption that produced it.** I reasoned *"these configs are grass-less, so they only need the
prep call"* — a plausible-sounding inference I never checked. ⛔ **Flannery is ALSO grass-less and
still gets all three lines.** One grep of the precedent would have settled it.
⇒ ⭐ **Prevention rule: when you copy a pattern, copy it WHOLE, or state in writing which part you
dropped and why. A pattern is a claim about what must happen together.**

**And a second defect I found while fixing the first, which the review had not reached.** Every
binding of `_lead_best_matchup`/`heal_in_pokemon_center` inside `_play` sits INSIDE an
`if not _done("BADGEnn_GET")` branch. A run RESUMING at badge 7 executes none of them, and a
function-local import makes the name function-local for the WHOLE function ⇒ my new calls would have
raised `UnboundLocalError` **on exactly the runs the change exists to help**. Fixed with a local
import at each site, which is why every existing site has one.
⇒ ‼ *The conditional-import trap has now bitten this file four times (three on `console`).*

⛔ **AND THE GATE I WROTE TO PROVE THIS DID NOT CATCH IT.** `probe_late_boss_configs.py` v1 checked
only the config DICT LITERALS and reported 6/6 PASS while the call sites were wrong.
⇒ ⭐⭐ **A GATE OVER DATA CANNOT VOUCH FOR THE CODE THAT USES THE DATA.** Fixed by adding case C7
(call-site wiring + the local import) with its own `=wiring` arm that reproduces the rejected draft.
‼ C7's FIRST implementation then false-failed on the block with the longer comment — a 1,800-char
window — i.e. it punished documentation. Now bounded structurally at the chapter dispatch.

**Also corrected the same day, same root cause (asserting a mechanism unverified):** I wrote in the
changelog that `grass_is_fodder` "is the sole gate on `_boss_plan_is_hopeless`/`_counter_ladder`".
FALSE — `story_mode.py:2284` reads `if boss_teaches:  # ⛔ KI-80: NOT `grass_is_fodder and …``; that
coupling was removed on 2026-08-16. I read gate #14's PURPOSE and inferred its CURRENT mechanism.
⇒ the "two independent arguments" for grass-less collapse to ONE (the L28 ceiling), which is
sufficient alone — and that sufficiency is exactly why the false second argument was easy to believe.

before Python ever sees the string. The file lands with each code span silently EXECUTED and
replaced by empty output: *"the  fence, the post-Winona / configs, ...  is the AUTHORITY"*.

**It happened twice today.** First on `07-CHANGELOG.md` (repaired with a `fix_changelog.py` script),
then again on `04-HANDOFF.md`'s STATE drift row — after I had already diagnosed it, written the
repair, and moved on. The fix I applied the first time was to that INSTANCE, not to my HABIT.

**Root cause.** Two write styles were in use and only one is safe:
* `py -3.12 - <<'PY' … PY`  (quoted heredoc) — safe, bash expands nothing. Used successfully ~8 times.
* `py -3.12 -c "…"`         — UNSAFE for any text containing backticks. Used twice; failed twice.
The two look equally routine at the call site, which is exactly why the unsafe one kept getting
picked — nothing distinguishes them until the damage is in the file.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *Markdown containing backticks is written from a FILE or a quoted
heredoc — NEVER from `-c "..."`. If the text has a code span, the double-quoted form is wrong.*

‼ **AND THE PART WORTH MORE THAN THE RULE: a gate caught the blast radius I did not look for.**
Repairing the row, `audit_doc_consistency.py` failed with THREE *other* cells still claiming
`drift=6` (`04-HANDOFF.md:677`, `:855`, `:891`) — stale the moment the promotion landed, and none of
them anywhere near the row I was editing. I would have fixed my own damage and shipped three false
claims.
⇒ **A mechanical gate is how you find the halves of a fact you did not know existed.** This is the
same P5 shape as the `18 cases` / `:1612` miss earlier today — a fact living in four places, and I
knew about one.
